I understand further that this same Inspector Dawson, to whom had been deputed the sacred task and duty of preserving intact and pure the administration of justice in this matter, is directly contradicted when he says he received a telegram addressed to him, G. W. Dawson. It is also a new and unreported fact that this Bill Miner was allowed to grow his whiskers and his hair. The Solicitor General says, as if he had made an actual measurement of the man's whiskers, that they were not longer than three-quarters of an inch. I do not think the administration of justice is dependent on whether these whiskers

were allowed to grow three-quarters of an inch, an inch or a foot, they were allowed to grow contrary to the penitentiary regulations of Canada. If I understand the Department of Justice aright, that fact was not brought to the attention of the department. In the light of all this new evidence, of all these material facts discovered since the investigation made by the man against whom all circumstantial evidence points as the man who was derelict in his duty, since this investigation was made by the culprit in the case, according to the circumstantial evidence in the case, surely no government in Canada will dare to ignore these important and material facts freshly discovered. Surely no man impressed with the importance of preserving pure and undefiled the administration of justice in Canada will dare to say:	We
will not accord an investigation. If we are reduced in Canada to the condition that men, fearful of their partisan advantage, fearful of the exposure of their own officers, fearful of I know not what else, refuse to permit an inquiry, then the administration of justice in the United States, at which we have been in the habit of pointing the finger of scorn, is away and above our own, our own which will set free a man convicted of the most serious crime in the calendar, a crime which has no parallel in the criminal annals of this country. I cannot believe that the government of Canada, impressed with the great obligation that is upon them, will dare in the light of these new facts to sit quiescent and refuse an investigation.

But for the evident attempt of the Minister of Justice to place the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. J. D. Taylor) in an improper light before the House, I would not have uttered a word to-day. The offence of the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. J. D. Taylor) is that he has unearthed the very suspicious circumstances connected with the escape of this man, Bill Miner, and forsooth, because the hon. member's paper chanced in copying from another paper to get the name of Macintosh instead of Mackenzie, we have the tirade against our friend which we have just heard. What is the object of all this bluster? Is it to so intimidate our friend from New Westminster that he will sit quietly in his seat like a good little boy the rest of the session and not dare to further seek to expose the gentlemen who have had charge of the management of this institution and of this particular case? The statements made by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. J. D. Taylor) were that Bill Miner's moustache was allowed to grow. It transpired that this was the case. Might I ask that the Minister of Justice follow this matter up to see by whose authority the order was given
which allowed this poor man, whose eyes were affected to grow his moustache? Is it or is it not true that the electric light in his cell so affected the nerves of the brain of the poor fellow that he could not sleep, and that after inquiry an order was given that Bill Miner's hair should be allowed to grow? We have it on the authority of the Solicitor General that it was at the time of his escape three-quarters of an inch long.
I said less than that.

Is it true that the orders of the Justice Department were deliberately violated in allowing this man to go from the inner inclosure into the brick yard where life prisoners axe never allowed? Is it true that poor Bill Miner's feet got sore walking around on the hard floor of the inner inclosure, and that by some authority he was allowed into the brickyard where his feet might rest on mother earth and bis corns might not cause him sleepless nights? Is it true that all these things followed the sercet interviews of these detectives? Is it or is it not true that immediately after the escape of Bill Miner the deputy warden who was acting as warden because the warden unfortunately was ill, wired the Department of Justice that four prisoners had escaped? Is it true, or is it not true, that the very following morning Bourke again wired the department that four prisoners-naming Miner among them -had escaped, and asking authority to offer a reward for their recapture?-this telegram addressed, not as the Minister of Justice has said, to one of the inspectors by name, but, according to Bourke's solemn statement to the Inspectors. If these facts be true, and if they have been produced subsequent to the inquiry, then if the Minister of Justice is anxious to allay public feeling, and if he dare cross the path of this man Bourke, there is only one way to proceed, and that is to order an investigation. We have all seen in the advertisements the contrasted pictures, ' Before taking ' and ' After taking.' We had a picture of the Minister of Justice standing in the House telling us that he had demanded, instantly demanded, of this man Bourke to produce his evidence. We have the other picture now of the minister standing hat in hand and saying: Please, Mr. Bourke, will you give us whatever data you have in connection with this affair that have not been brought out. The case strikes the public as very strange and very suspicious. The public want to know how it happens that Bourke is the master of the situation. Another point on which the Minister of Justice is in error, in addition to those pointed out by the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) and the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) is this: he endeavoured to make a point against my hon.

friend from New Westminster (Mr. J. D Taylor) by saying that escapes had occurred that year previous to Bill Miner's. The records do not show it. And the minister explains his mistake by saying that recaptures were not reported. Well, let us see. I have the minister's report before me, and at page 2 1 find a statement that, in 1904-1905, there were three escapes and, at the foot is a note stating that one of [DOT] those who escaped was recaptured. In 1905, two prisoners escaped and it is stated that both were recaptured. The minister talks a little too fast, and not by his own book. A trifling mistake in a name-between Macintosh and McKenzie, both good Scotch names,-was not sufficient to justify the Minister of Justice in reading the Riot Act, as he has done, to the member for New Westminster. If the Minister of Justice considers his own personal and political credit, if he values the administration of justice in this country and has any desire to satisfy an honest public, and if he is not under the thumb of this man Bourke- I say that advisedly, if he is not under the thumb of this man Bourke-then, to my mind, there is only one course open to him, and that is to bring these parties before a committee of this House and have a full and fair inquiry so that these rumours may be set at rest and the truth may be made known.

Answering the hon. member from New Westminster (Mr. J. D. Taylor) the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) seemed to make much of the fact that the escape was investigated by Mr. Dawson the inspector of penitentiaries. At the time Mr. Dawson was appointed to make this investigation, Mr. Bourke was the superintendent of the prison at New Westminster, and it was under Mr. Bourke, as superintendent, that the prisoners had escaped. After the investigation had been made and after-according to the Minister of Justice-Mr. Dawson hail reported that there was no blame attached to the superintendent of the prison, we find that the superintendent was superannuated. And the Minister of Justice, referring to this superannuation made very much of the point that, notwithstanding the fact that he had been negligent of his duty and had openly violated the rules of held, Mr. Dawson was Mr. Bourke's superior annuated at the full allowance for his term of service, and the minister seemed to put that forward as a reason why no complaint should be made by the superintendent of the prison. But when the investigation was held Mr. Dawson was Mr. Bourke's superior officer, and he, Mr. Bourke, had reason to believe that if the explanation he gave was satisfactory to Mr. Dawson he would be maintained in his position and it was only Mr. HUGHES.
after he had been superannuated at lesser salary than he thought he was entitled to that he made the various statements that had been published from time to time. That is most important. The Minister of Justice writes, not demanding anything from Mr. Bourke, but, as the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) has said, in a somewhat pleading strain, asking Mr. Bourke if he had stated all the facts in the investigation prior to his superannuation. And Mr. Bourke, as has been pointed out, rather curtly replies that he had done so. But, in his signed statement in the newspapers of the province, Mr. Bourke has stated that, if asked to do so before an independent commission appointed to investigate this question, he could tell many things that he had not told previously. And the minister makes a complaint in regard to this; he pleads that it is very unfair on the part of a man treated so well by the government to make statements of this kind. But the real question is that raised, by the leader of the opposition: These statements are either true or not true; if true, they call for an investigation, and Mr. Bourke is still a servant of the people in that he is in receipt of pay as a superannuated servant; if not true, he should declare before an independent tribunal that these statements are not correct so that the Department of Justice may be free from suspicion. It has been truly said that the whole government of our country hangs on the purity of our administration of justice. If we fail in that, all our government fails. This is not a small matter, and I am surprised that the head of the Justice Department, should, on a question of this kind, declare that lie has given all the information necessary and that he sees no cause for further investigation. I do not intend to go further into this subject, but I think the two points, the real points at issue, are those raised by the leader of the opposition, and that this House should demand a full investigation by an independent authority into the escape of this prisoner.

My hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. J. D. Taylor) is a new member of this House, and perhaps he will not take it amiss from me, who have had more experience than he in parliamentary practice, if I tell him that, in view of the discussion he wished to introduce and the information he wished to elicit, it would have been preferable if he had followed the usual practice when a matter of this kind is to be brought under discussion, and had notified the parties interested of his intention, so that they might have been prepared with the documents to meet any statements that he might make. As I understand, he did not take that pre-

caution, and therefore the discussion cannot be as complete as it would be otherwise. Had we had notice of his intention, we could have had documents at hand to meet the views he presented to the House.
I may say that a good deal of matter has been brought into this discussion* which seems to me absolutely irrelevant to the question. The question which interests the country-and the only question in which the country is interested-is, whether there has been any connivance on the part of anybody in the escape of Miner. No more dangerous criminal, I think, was ever in the clutches of Canadian justice.
It was a fact for which we took some credit that when one of these American desperadoes came to Canada, thinking to play with impunity in this country the pranks he had been playing on the other side of the line, he was arrested, tried and convicted. It was a shock when we heard, and we heard it with a good deal of shame also, that he had subsequently been allowed to escape from the penitentiary. If the discussion had been confined to these facts I would have more sympathy than I now have with the manner in which it has been brought to the attention of the House. I think a good deal of the matter brought forward has-been irrelevant. I agree with the hon. member for Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Burrell) that it is not of much importance that, in despatches which are sent to British Columbia newspapers, the name Macintosh had been substituted for the name Mackenzie. That in itself would be of no consequence, but it is of some consequence in this matter. I would say to my hon. friend from New Westminster that since he is the responsible editor of the paper in which the mistake occurred, and if he intended to bring the matter before the House, it would have been perhaps better and more in accordance with the courtesy, with the etiquette and the amenity of public life, if he had taken the opportunity of correcting that mistake. Telegrams, in transmission from the sender to the receiver, may get distorted, we have had evidences of that before; but I think it is due to the person who has been misrepresented that the editor should take the opportunity of correcting the error. In this case my hon. fiiend did not choose to do so, and so I say the substitution of the name Macintosh was not without some importance in relation to the matter under discussion, because the fact that the name Macintosh was inro-duced in this telegram gave to the newspaper an opportunity of going to see Mr. Mackenzie and getting from him what I cannot characterize otherwise than a tirade against the Department of Justice. Therefore it would have been better, in the interest of the administration of justice generally, and in the interest of truth, if the
error had been corrected there. It was not corrected.
What was the date?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: 18th of February. My hon. friend, in the course of his observations, tried to cast a slur upon the investigation which took place-at all events I assume that was his intention, from the statement he made later on. He wanted to give the impression, an impression which seems to prevail on .the other side of the House, according to the speeches we have heard this afternoon, that the investigation which has taken place had not been as full and as complete as it might have been. He read from a newspaper-I am sorry I could not hear very well what he read, but I understood him to read from an interview in which some one stated that if he had been called upon he would have shown that Bill Miner had not escaped through a wall, and that he would have shown how he had escaped. Now, Sir, I ask my hon. friend, and I ask the House generally, what importance or what reliance can be attached to such a statement as that? Hon. gentlemen have tried to show that the investigation which took place at Dawson into the manner in which Miner had escaped, was not as complete as it might have been, because a certain man had stated that if he had been called upon he could have thrown light upon the manner of the escape. But if I understood my hon. friend aright, the extract which he read did not give the name of that man. Am I right?
It said a high official, without naming him.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Well, how are we to know who this high official was? It is contended that there should be a new investigation. On this point I express no oninion, the matter is new to me. But it is not possible to come to a conclusion on a vague statement of that kind. If a newspaper says that somebody is able to give certain information, surely nobody would pretend that such a statement is a sufficient basis for a further inquiry. Now I appeal to hon. members on both sides of this House whether it is advantageous to the administration of justice, advantageous to the administration of any other department of the government, that we should have these slurs cast from one side of the House or the other; I say that at least we should have some responsible name put forward as a basis for any further investigation. If we are shown any reason to suppose that the investigation was not as complete as it possibly could be, that further facts might be discovered to show how this man escaped, then I would be willing to go very far in order to find that out. But it is not possible for any reasonable man to come to any other conclusion than that we have ob-

tained the whole truth in regard to this matter, so far as it can be obtained. I wish we had more information. So far as I can see, the administration of justice in that respect was loose, and the department has, I understand, taken the precaution to put it in better hands. I do not know what mistake has been made, but I am ready to agree with the hon. member for New Westminster that the administration of the penitentiary was not what it should be, it was carried on in a manner that called for correction, and it has since been corrected. But so far as I can see, I put it to the good sense of the House whether any case has been made for another investigation). I think that charges most unfair have been made against the minister himself, who is a painstaking official, and a credit to the administration of justice in Canada, and who could have nothing but a stern desire to meet any deficiency that was found to exist in the administration of the penitentiaries under his charge.

The Prime Minister has very cooly and dispassionately discussed the question for a brief period, and I suppose that we may with equal coolness and dispassionateness discuss what the Prime Minister has said. He commenced by lecturing a new member. New members do not know the order of the debate as well as older members, and they ought to be excused for not adhering strictly to its forms. So I think the Prime Minister might have excused the member without parading the offence. It is right that when you are going to bring up an important matter, the minister who is in charge of the department affected should be informed of it, with a view of eliciting the utmost information. My hon. friend from New Westminster, a new member, forgot that; but I have known even older members to forget it and to bring up matters without notice. Of course it is not absolutely a rule of the House, it is a courtesy which is generally observed, because it ends by forwarding the purpose had in view. So much with reference to the lecture which was read to the member for New Westminster. Then the Prime Minister deplored irrelevant matter having been introduced into this discussion. It was deplorable, there is no doubt about that. But who is the man that introduced that irrelevant matter? The man who introduced it, and added all the acerbity that has been imported into this debate, sits exactly behind the Prime Minister. Here is my hon. friend from New Westminster, why should he have been reproached by a Minister of Justice with having undue relations with a newspaper, and using it-well, to say the least, somewhat dishonestly. No other inference could be taken from the words of the Minister of Justice. It is certainly no disgrace, it is no dishonour, and I do not think it is any Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
great disadvantage to a man to represent in this House his constituency and at the same time be the editor, or proprietor, or owner of a newspaper. But the gravamen of the charge that was made by the Minister of Justice, made with malice aforethought, was that this hon. gentleman having a newspaper here, indited a telegraphic despatch to that newspaper intended to and which actually did misrepresent the Minister of Justice, and that, on this basis of misrepresentation, the newspaper published interviews and comments which were derogatory to the Minister of Justice and to the management of his department. I ask the Prime Minister if he can get any other meaning from the words that the Minister of Justice used? There is no use in labouring that point. That is actually what the Minister of Justice said, and his statement was as plain as a pikestaff, that this was wrong in that paper whilst in other papers it was correct.

In all other
newspapers?

Whether he said all newspapers in the province or not I will not say but he said that in the other newspapers the despatch was correct. When the Minister of Justice, instead of adhering closely and dispassionately to the facts of the case, starts out to try to injure a member who, in the course of his duty, brings up the matter, when he does this on a wrong basis of facts and, when as he afterwards acknowledged, he had not himself taken the precaution to verify these facts, he' did something that he was not justified in doing. That is where the trouble arose in this debate. The Minister of Justice is prone to do that sort of thing. Yesterday furnished an example, other days have furnished other examples and it would be well for the department and more in keeping with its traditions if the Minister of Justice would leave a little of his petty partisanship to one side and treat his political opponents with more fairness. It was a shock and a shame, said the Prime Minister, to learn that Bill Miner had escaped as it was with joy and pride that they learned that Canadian officers and Canadian courts had been instrumental in catching such a noted desperado and afterwards, by the machinery of the law, in landing him in prison for life. The position of matters was well defined. The Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister were glad that Bill Miner the desperado, had been landed within the penitentiary at New Westminster. The Minister of Justice knew that Bill Miner, a noted desperado, was in the penitentiary, he knew that the discipline was bad in the penitentiary, he knew that just previously to his receiving certain information one, two, three prisoners had escaped therefrom.
1853 MARCH 2, 1909 1854	
All this he knew when he received, on the 8th day of August, notice that four prisoners had escaped out of the New Westminster penitentiary. The Minister of Justice, with all that pre-added knowledge and consciousness, did not take enough interest in the matter to immediately inquire about the names and the circumstances. Four days elapse and still he had not inquired. What is the mildest name that one could give to inaction of that kind ? I think that there was an initial negligence and a lack of that proper promptness which should characterize the department under such circumstances as those. Now, we go a little further. The Prime Minister says that my hon. friend should have corrected his mistake. My hon. friend, the member for New Westminster, was in Ottawa city. The telegram went to the paper in British Columbia. On the 18th it was published in that paper. My hon. friend did not see that paper again until certainly a week and maybe more had passed. He had no data for correcting the mistake at least until the paper came within his hands. I do not know how many days after the 18th it did come. I do not know the date of the publishing of the paper but the probabilities are that he would not see this paper until four, five, six or seven days after his telegram appeared. Then, my hon. friend says that he communicated with the man himself, Mr. Macintosh, and told him that it was a mistake. It might have been quick and prompt if the man and the newspaper had been on the same street. It was absolutely impossible to make it either quick or prompt with half a continent intervening between the two. Now, the Prime Minister says that we have nothing upon which to base a renewed investigation. Why? Is there any good reason why, if there is a scintilla of new evidence, it should not be followed up? Circumstances that have been detailed here to-day in reference to the bonds, the lax discipline, the visits against the various rules of the department, the fact that these visits were known to the inspector of the department, and that they did not come, by way of a report from that inspector to the department, calls for an investigation. This is a fact, if I understand the facts correctly. I will leave myself to be corrected with regard to that but that is the way I understand it. Am I wrong in that? Mr. BUREAU. I do not know if I understand my hon. friend. Does he mean to say that the inspector was aware of the visits before he held the investigation in New Westminster? The inspector only learned of these things after he had held the investigation, as I am informed. Mr. FOSTER. That is the only point about which I was uncertain and that is	why I made the inquiry. Then, as I understand it, these visits are recorded in the books at the penitentiary. Mr. BUREAU. Some of them are in the book, as was stated by the minister in his answer which appeared in ' Hansard ' on the 17th of February. All those that are entered are mentioned there. I am informed that four are entered and one is not. Mr. FOSTER. Some of the entries of visits refer to visits to Bill Miner? Mr. BUREAU. Yes. Mr. FOSTER. Then, as I understand it, the inspector was there and if he inspected anything he would inspect the books. If he had inspected the books he would have found the record of these visits, he would have made some inquiry about them and he would have reported that inquiry back to the department. But, those visits were not reported by the inspector. These then are the facts. The escaped prisoner has not been taken. And now there come up two pieces of evidence. Reference has been made to the name of an official of high authority, who has been quoted by a newspaper as having definite information, which, if he had been aksed for it, would have thrown a very different light upon this question. The man's name is not given, but the paper referred to is the 'Province,' which is, I understand, a responsible and very reputaDie paper. Sir WILFRID LAURIER. I do not understand that there is any name given in the newspaper. Mr. FOSTER. I did not say that the name is there; I stated that the statement appears in the newspaper and that the newspaper stated that he was a high official. Does not the Prime Minister think that something to go upon especially in a case like this? Is the minister of the department to take no cognizance of that at all by way of a communication with the newspaper publisher asking him for the name of that high official? As it stands it is a blot and an asipersion upon the name of that particular penitentiary. A statement made in a. reputable newspaper that a high official is in a position to give further evidence and make further disclosures, is a thing that the Department of Justice should follow up. The Department of Justice says it will not do sq because it cannot take cognizance of an anonymous statement, but if the Department of Justice wants to follow it up X have no doubt a method can be found to do so. More than that, Mr. Bourke is your own official; he was there at the time of the escape; it was he and the late departed warden who allowed the rules to be transgressed; he is cognizant of these negotiations if any went

on, and his latest statement is -that he is able to give information which will put a very different light upon this matter. We are not inclined to make a partisan question of the administration of the Department of Justice or the discipline in one of our great penitentiaries. My hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) did not start out in that way. He was fallen foul of by the Minister of Justice, who in most excited language and stentorian tones belaboured the member for New Westminster for bringing the matter up at all. It is that which added the spice of bitterness to this debate and but for that there would have been nothing partisan about it. We will forgive the Minister of Justice-it is his failing perhaps more than his fault-but desiring as we do on both sides of the House that the matter should be cleared up, is there not good ground now for further investigation? If the idea goes abroad that prisoners may escape from our penitentiaries that is bad enough; but, if the idea goes abroad that they can escape by connivance that is worse, and if in addition there is a suspicion in the public mind that that connivance was built upon financial or moneyed interest that makes it still worse. It seems to me it is necessary to pursue this investigation in view of the added evidence. Bring Mr. Bourke before a competent examining authority and get from him the new evidence he has or make him show he has not got it. Get, if possible, the high official who is said to have communicated with the 'Province' newspaper and let us, as far as we possibly can, have the matter set at rest. It is of so much importance and means so much for the good name of our administration of justice in Canada that in my opinion it cannot be left where it is.

The discussion this afternoon must have struck any one who listened to it with any degree of care as one of those peculiar occasions which sometimes, during the last three or four years, have developed in this parliament when gentlemen on the other side have started discussions based upon mere newspaper rumour. I am afraid that the Minister of Justice rather stirred up hon gentlemen on the other side by his references to the unreliability of the telegrams which are published in certain British Columbia newspapers, and hence we have had all kinds of forebodings and all kinds of suggestions about wrong-doing and the necessity for an investigation into this and into that. But let us look at the question calmly. Bill Miner escaped from the British Columbia penitentiary in August, 1907, the man in charge of the penitentiary being the deputy warden, the warden being ill at the time. There is some question as to the non-delivery of a telegram which was Mr. POSTER.
addressed to Inspector Dawson at Ottawa, and some hon. gentlemen have endeavoured to cast so much suspicion on Inspector Dawson, that you would think Inspector Dawson was in British Columbia conspiring for the escape of Miner. At all events, owing to a peculiarity about these British Columbia telegrams, there was a non-delivery of the message announcing that Miner had escaped. But as soon as Mr. Dawson did receive the information he proceeded to British Columbia, held an investigation into the facts; an investigation similar in all respects to that which was held by every Minister of Justice when the Conservatives were in power and when they also had escapes from the penitentiaries. I am reminded by the Minister of Justice that under the Penitentiary Act which has been on the statute book for a great number of years, the inspector was the official who alone could conduct an investigation into the matter. That investigation was held, and as a result of it the inspector recommended that the deputy warden who was in charge of the penitentiary at the time should be allowed to retire and that the guard should be retired. The government accepted these recommendations. Now, the hon. gentleman from New Westminster has on two occasions precipitated discussion with regard to this matter without the slightest reason. You would think to have heard these hon. gentlemen opposite this afternoon that some one of them had moved for the papers and had them brought down and that the official record of all the proceedings had been placed upon the table of the House, so that every hon. member, and the country, and the newspapers might at least know what had been done in the matter. But my hon. friend from New Westminster has not done that.
Will the hon. gentleman permit me to say that I moved for these papers and the motion was carried about two weeks ago.

Then my hon. friend, in the style of so many other members on that side of the House, proceeded to discuss the subject before the papers were brought down and without knowing the facts. Had he only waited until the official documents in regard to this matter were laid on the table of this House and he in common with every other member of the House had an opportunity to read them, then it would have been possible for us to give the matter the serious and practical consideration that it deserves.
Do those papers change the facts as stated by the Minister of Justice?

My hon. friend was one of the gentlemen who applauded most vociferously when his hon.

friends talked about an investigation. Like him, I have no knowledge of what the papers contain, but I am prepared to wait till they come down before I take the responsibility of saying what should be done. My hon. friend the Solicitor General informs me that there is no record of the motion which my hon. friend from New Westminster states he made. But he can take that matter up at another time.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to order. I have made the statement that a motion of mine was carried in this House, and the hon. gentleman quotes the Solicitor General as flatly contradicting me. My statement is perfectly correct, and the Minister of Justice made an address to this House on the motion.

For the purpose of my argument it is of no importance whatever whether the hon. gentleman made the motion or not, because if he did, lie should have paid some deference to the intelligence of the members of this House and waited till the pacers should be brought down before discussing the question, so that every hon. member should know what he was discussing.
Retract.

subtopic: CANADIAN LIVERPOOL AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, I am at a loss to understand why this section should be struck out. The mere fact of this Bill being before the House, after having been sent to the Railway Gommittee, and of its asking that civil and legal rights be conferred upon a railway, is a prima facie evidence that this parliament is entitled to legislate upon this matter. It is incumbent upon those who oppose this section, to show that the whole Bill or some part of it does not come within the province of parliament. However, I believe that it is in the public interest and conducive to the proper management of the affairs of the Dominion that such a clause be inserted in all the bills.
The hon. member for Terrebonne, is apparently of the belief that this is a new clause inserted in charters incorporating companies. On the contrary, it is the usual clause, and whoever is familiar with judicial matters is perfectly aware of it. There is no need for its justification. The Brit- [DOT] Mr. E. M. MACDONALD.
ish North America Act, distinctly states that whatever is outside the exclusive jurisdiction of the provincial legislature, falls within the scope of the powers of the Dominion parliament. It is incumbent on the opponents of this clause to show that the Bill deals with a matter exclusively within the scope of the powers of the legislature. If that is not shown, jurisdiction is implied. It has been stated that no proof had been given, that such an enterprise was for the advantage of Canada as a whole. Such evidence has not been asked for by any one. The law does not require it. The clauses inserted in the Bill are in themselves sufficient evidence that it falls within the scope of the federal author-ityf Were similar clauses inserted in a Bill submitted to the Quebec legislature, there would be sufficient ground for warranting its cancellation.
Let us take, for instance, clause 13, which reads as follows :
13. Subject to the provisions of sections 361, 362 and 363 of The Railway Act, the Company may, for any of the purposes specified in the said section 361, enter into agreements with the Transcontinental Railway Company, The Grand Trunk Kailway Company, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, the Canadian Northern Quebec Railway Company, or any of them.
To my mind, that power of entering into agreements with railway companies which are under the control of the Dominion government, implies that of establishing connections between those various railroads and gives parliament jurisdiction.
It is alleged that this company asked authority to build and run a railway wholly within the limits of the province of Quebec. My answer is that it is not solely the territory covered by the railway which should be considered, when the question of jurisdiction is to be decided. It is necessary, besides, that the powers applied for by the company should be such as the legislature has authority to grant. Whenever the powers, rights or privileges dealt with are not exclusively under the control of a legislature, the Bill falls within the scope of federal authority.
There is no need for my quoting any further from the Bill, since all its clauses are known to hon. members, who have made a study of it, as for instance, that relative to navigation and commerce. How could the Quebec legislature be called upon to legislate on such questions ?
After carefully studying this Bill, I am bound to say that it does not concern some vital interests of the province of Quebec only, but that, considering the territory it runs through and the powers which the company requests this parliament to grant, the work may be stated to be for the general advantage of the Dominion. Nor shall I stop at that : I say that this

parliament has not only the right, but has for its duty to grant to the company the act of incorporation which they have applied for, and that it is in the interest of Canada that we should not be debarred from passing such legislation.
It would be a very dangerous precedent for us, as representatives of the people of this Dominion to assume an attitude of indifference towards such legislation, to refuse dealing with it and refer it back to the legislature of Quebec, it would amount to stating that all the clauses in this Bill are within the exclusive scope of provincial legislature. The discussion which has been carried on just now, has an interest far exceeding that of the mere incorporation of a railway company. It is a principle which we are about to lay down. I wonder whether our parliament is going cheerfully and deliberately to proclaim its lack of powers, without even having gone into the clauses of the Bill submitted to us, for it is a fact that we have reached the second clause only, out of a total of thirteen. Should some of the following sections deal exclusively with provincial matters, nothing prevents us from cancelling them or inserting a proviso safeguarding the rights of the legislature. In following a different course, we would, to my mind, be evading our duty and aiming a slur, as it were, at this parliament. As I said a moment ago, it would be creating a dangerous precedent, and I hope the House will not take such a responsibility.

That construtcion of the words has on many occasions enabled us to invade provincial rights. I was not present at the meetings of the Railway Committee when this Bill was under consideration, but I believe that one of the strongest arguments brought forward

against its acceptance was to the effect that no evidence had been adduced to show that such legislation was of interest to Canada as a whole; and it seemS to me that the position taken by the member for Terrebonne, in whose opinion proof should be furnished beforehand as to the character of the undertaking, in order to give us jurisdiction, cannot be controverted. I listened carefully to the arguments of the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Turcotte). He has not denied the fact. speechtext:
This Bill involves a question of provincial rights and has caused great discussion and loss of time in this House. It appears, as near as I can understand, that a few men can get together, chip in a few dollars, and having raised $300 or $400, they can come here and ask for a Bill giving them greater powers even than the provinces have. This is an omnibus Bill. In the first place, it is a railway charter, and I see no particular reason why, so far as that is concerned, the Bill should not pass. But there is added also a shipping clause, and this is added in order to have some argument to carry through the most dangerous clause in the Bill, namely, the water-power clause, under which the company may develop power and dispose of electrical energy. I think it is time that this House took a stand on this question, and, when gentlemen come here and ask for Bills of this character, we should compel them to separate the various powers asked for and then consider, straight and fair, each one as a separate Bill on its merits. Why is this water-power and electric light and power clause incorporated in a railway charter, seeing that it is recognized that these matters appertain to the province ? The reason, I take it, is that there is no expropriation power for these companies under provincial legislation. They come to this parliament for these expropriation powers, for the purpose of seizing water-powers which are now or will soon be, valuable. This is the most dangerous thing that can be asked. Why ? Because we give them power to invade private rights and even to seize and expropriate provincial properties. If I understand this Bill aright, it empowers these gentlemen to seize every water-power in the province of Quebec from Lake St. John to Montreal. Even though a water-power may be twenty miles away from the track and owned by a private individual, they can take it from the owner by expropriation. Even jf the province of Quebec owns a water-power fifty miles away from the railway, there is nothing to prevent the company seizing it and using it for their own purposes. It is not even provided that the railway must be
built before these powers of expropriation can be exercised by this company. I had an evidence of the apparent power behind this Bill in the Railway Committee. I realized for the first time what it was to have a lobby there in support of a Bill. I had been told before I came to this House that when a dangerous Bill was to be put through there was a strong lobby, and it was generally composed of members from the province of Quebec. I did not belie ye it until I saw the lobby behind this Bill with my own eyes. We saw some of these gentlemen from Quebec strenuously forwarding this Bill which takes away the right of their own province, rights which the province, through its representatives before the Railway Committee asked us not to interfere with by passing this Bill. I, as a representative from the province of Ontario, feel keenly on this subject, because the rights of my own province have been violated on a number of occasions by Bills of this kind. It is said that one of the most valuable undeveloped water-powers in Ontario has been expropriated-in fact, it took three or four railway charters from this House to cover all the available powers on a certain river in Ontario-in this way. It is high time when gentlemen ask for such powers as are proposed to be given under this Bill, that they should be called upon to give evidence of good faith. And, further, if representatives of the province of Quebec come here laying violent hands on the rights and property of their own province, they cannot expect the representatives of other provinces to have much sympathy for them when rights of even a more delicate character are in danger. They are establishing a dangerous principle. Every member of this House, no matter on which side he may be, should stand up for the rights of his province and of other provinces in matters of this kind. There is nothing very great at stake in this Bill. The promoters do not tell us: 'We have $3,000,000 or $4,000,000 in the bank ready to go on with this work.' It is purely a speculative paper charter. And when these gentlemen ask us to give them power to expropriate provincial water-powers and properties, they are going beyond the mark. The province of Quebec has no coal; in that respect, it is in the same position as the province of Ontario. In a few years, the wood will be gone. Coal will always be a high-priced article in the province of Quebec. How are you going to turn the wheels of your factories? How are your intelligent hard-working population, the best class of artisans in the world, to get employment in the province of Quebec, if you are going to give away your water-powers and tie them up in monopolies in this fashion ? It is clear that this Bill involves a very dangerous principle

and this House should reject it. Not only can they seize water-powers even from the province itself, but they can go into any city and deliver power.

I protest most energetically against the language that has been used by the hon. member towards the members from the province of Quebec, who understand their duties as well-I will not say even better-than the hon. gentleman himself does I say, as a member from that province, that I resent the language which has been used to qualify the conduct of Quebec members on the committee. The hon. gentleman says that after coming to this parliament he has had an opportunity of observing that the Quebec members were, to use his own words, purely and simply lobbyists, taking charge of whatever piece of legislation might come before the committee, and doing the work which ought to be performed by the promoters themselves in pushing those Bills through the committee and afterwards through the House.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I say there is not the least foundation, there is not the least excuse, for the language the hon. gentleman has used to-night. Every one of the members of my province resent that language, and feel it their duty, through my humble voice, to make a most energetic and formal protest against it. As members of the Railway Committee, hon. gentlemen coming from the province of Quebec, as well as from the other provinces, understand that there is only one thing to do when a Bill is brought before the Railway Committee, and that is to study the Bill upon its merits, and if they find it based upon a just and sound principle, to support it irrespective of every other consideration. The hon. member has just hinted, in fact he has plainly intimated, that other considerations than those of public interest actuate the members from the province of Quebec in studying any piece of legislation that comes before the Railway Committee and the House. Well, I can only repeat that there is not the least ground for such an accusation as the hon. member has seen fit to make tonight.
Now, coming to the Bill which is before us, I, as a member of the Railway Committee, took some part in the consideration of this legislation when the Bill came before the committee for the first time. I thought that it was one that fell properly within the jurisdiction of this parliament, not only because in clause 2 the works of the company are declared to be for the general advantage of Canada, but because many other provisions of the Bill bring it within the jurisdiction of this parliament. Irrespective of any other consideration, looking at the object of the Bill from a public standpoint, I said to myself, as every other member of

the committee should say to himself, that it was my duty to support it and to see that it was adopted by the committee and by the House. Now I will not go over the arguments, which have been pretty well set forth by members who have previously spoken. But I can say that I feel at perfect liberty to vote for the Bill for the reasons which have been given by my hon. friend from Quebec, and by my hon. friend from St. Johns. Finally, I desire to say once more that the members of my province resent the imputation made by the hon. member, which was altogether unfounded, and I protest against such language, not only on my own behalf, but on behalf of all the members of the Railway Committee coming from the province of Quebec.

speechtext: What is the evidence that the hon. gentleman thinks would warrant us in saying that this is a work for the general advantage of Canada?

speechtext: The 8th clause of the Bill provides for the building of a line which is to be connected with other lines under the jurisdiction of this parliament. Under clause 13 of the Bill, the promoters of the company ask for power to enter into agreements with the Transcontinental Railway Company, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, the Grand Trunk Railway Company, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, the Canadian Northern Quebec Railway Company, or any of them. All these companies have been created by this parliament, and it is obvious that the promoters of this Bill require authority from this parliament to enter into agreements with these other companies, because their line starts from a point on one of them, the Transcontinental Railway. There are other clauses which justify the promoters coming before this parliament for incorporation. It seems to me that the opposition which is offered to the Bill is not inspired by motives of public interest. We know very well what hon. gentlemen think when they talk about provincial autonomy.

subtopic: CANADIAN LIVERPOOL AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
In reference to what the hon. gentleman says, I am not so touchy about dealing with this subject as he appears to be. I would say that the last statement the hon. gentleman made was entirely unwarranted, when he insinuates that any member of this House is actuated by other than public motives. However, I do not care what he says about it, because it does not make any difference. I would point out that section 8 of the Railway Act is ample security, for all they want to get in a provincial charter. They have in the Railway Act that section which provides that the jurisdiction of the Railway Commissioners shall apply for all necessary purposes, and even to provincial railways which connect with Dominion railways.
That is why I asked the hon. gentleman where was the evidence which would warrant us in deciding the question of fact. Now I am not like other gentlemen in the Railway Committee, who assume at once, whenever a charter is asked for in this House, that the work is for the general advantage of Canada. By the way we have been acting for the last few years we have got that principle turned upside down. We keep on deciding without any evidence whatever that the work is for the general advantage of Canada, whereas before we have any constitutional right to incorporate a company, the onus is on the promoters to present us with the evidence. We keep on in the Railway Committee, that is the majority of us, and I do not belong to the majority, deciding without a tittle of evidence that the work is for the general advantage of Canada. No other tribunal would decide any such thing, the onus being upon the applicants to convince us as a parliamentary committee that there is an exceptional reason why a certain matter cannot be dealt with under the clause of the British Noith America Act which gives the provinces jurisdiction, forgetting, and wilfully forgetting, apparently, that under the British North America Act railways are primarily within the jurisdiction of the provinces.
It is only when we have evidence before us which is substantial, which is convincing, that a provincial charter will not serve the purpose sought for that we have the right to decide that the work should have Dominion incorporation and be declared to be a work for the general advantage of Canada. I did it in the last parliament, and again I am going to enter my protest against this sort of thing. We are shirking our duty; we are undertaking to decide a fact to be in the affirmative without any evidence of it. Hon. gentlemen seem to confuse the questions of power and duty. Over and over again it is said in the Railway Committee, and sometimes in this House, that we have the power, if we declare this work to be a work for the general advantage of Canada, to incorporate a company. Nobody says we have not the power, but the question is: Have we exercised the power properly and judicially in making that declaration, and have we the evidence to wararnt us in deciding that question? In this case there is not a particle of evidence to warrant us in coming to that conclusion and without evidence to show that this is a work that cannot be properly dealt with by the province of Quebec we should not sanction this incorporation. I care not which province may be concerned. I cannot help it if hon. gentlemen from the province of Quebec are going to get angry because this happens to come from their province. They must not do that and expect us to sympathize with them. We say the same thing with regard to protecting any other province in the

Dominion. We are consistent at all events upon this question. Whether this comes from Quebec or any other province the fact is the same, that if there is no evidence to warrant us in coming to such a conclusion as would justify us with any sort of a judicial mind in deciding that it is a work for the general advantage of Canada I am not prepared to vote for the Bill.

There is no point of order in that, and I did not hear the hon. member for North Simcoe utter any such language as that. Any man who, in this House, wants to safeguard the rights of the province of Quebec in a matter of this kind and to assure to that province the control of its important water-powers, for the reasons indicated by my hon. friend from North Simcoe, is entitled to the credit of the province, and if he displays some heat in advocating these rights he may rest assured that those who realize what the needs of our province are will be thankful for it. . I desire to refer for a moment to what was said by the hon. member for Chicoutimi and Saguenay (Mr. Girard), who stated that on forty-two different occasions, to his own knowledge, I had been a party to such legislation and approved of it. I was not aware that the hon. gentleman had followed so carefully my delinquencies in this House. Upon that score I have a very tranquil conscience, because, if I sinned forty-two times I sinned in company with my hon. friend.
I am free to confess that what has been stated here to-night by one member of this committee, that in the past we have been a great deal too lax in matters of this kind, is well founded. It has been so for a long time and I think it is time to see to it that the rights of the provinces are safeguarded. There is the instance of the railway on the Island of Montreal. Upon what proof was this declared to be a railwav for the general advantage of Canada, confined as it is to the Island of Montreal and therefore falling under the jurisdiction of this parliament? I question very much indeed if it is to the advantage of the city of Montreal or of the province generally. Has there been any proof adduced that this projected company is a company in the general interest of Canada? That is the only clause in the whole charter that gives us any jurisdiction. Is there a member of this committee who will say that if there has been no proof of that, this parliament is not committing a rash act in incorporating this company? What proof, have we, Sir, that in view of the protest which was lodged before the Railway Committee by the province of Quebec, through its authorized attorney, who said that they did not wish to see this legislation passed, this company has not come here because it knew that the parliament at Quebec would not grant the privileges it is claiming for us? We are arrogating a jurisdiction to ourselves, and the point raised by my hon. friend from North Simcoe is a particularly interesting one for us in the province of Quebec. If we assume jurisdiction and give to this comnanv the power which is mentioned in clause 38 of expropriating water-powers for the development of electricity we will place

the province of Quebec, which has no coal and which has such a wealth of hydraulic power, in the most unfair position which will give rise to trouble later on. Under these circumstances, it seems to me that we should at least refer it hack to the committee in order that ample proof should be secured of the general interest which has been alleged by speakers in favour of this Bill, but of which no proof whatever has been given.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. W. MADDIN (South Cape Breton).
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before coming to this House as a representative I had a full recognition of the great differences dividing the political parties on matters of policy and such like, but I had to wait until today to find that an important matter such as the escape of a life sentenced desperado like Bill Miner would be a subject upon which the political parties in this country would differ. This matter is of too great significance to be dealt lightly with, and in view of its great importance I submit that the hon. gentleman (Mr. J. D. Taylor) who initiated the debate is not open to the censure visited on him by gentlemen opposite. I find in a recent edition of the Ottawa ' Free Press,' an organ of this government the following:

The conditions at the British Columbia penitentiary, which have been the subject of parliamentary comment within the past month should be investigated either by ft committee. of the House of Commons or by a judicial commission. That there is something radically wroag in that institution is proven not merely by the rumours and counter-rumours in circulation respecting the escape of Bill Miner and his accomplices, but also oy the fact that the past wees has seen a repetition of the jail breaking as a result of which two convicts got away, one of whom is still at large. That such a thing could happen after the experience with Miner, and especially after the re-organization of the penitentiary staff, shows that there is still need for more reforms.
Discipline is the first essential in a successful penitentiary, but discipline seems to be a much lacking commodity at New Westminster. The record of the past few years, including the escape of Miner, an insurrection or two among the conviots, several suicides, the practical dismissal of the former deputy warden and his replacement by a hospital steward, as well as the self-confessed trafficking in tobacco and other luxuries be tween the guards and the convicts-fill this certainly justifies a searching investigation The government has everything to gain and nothing to lose by a full and impartial investigation and we trust that the Minister of Justice urill soon see his way to ordering such an investigation.
I deplore, Mr. Speaker, that the conditions which in this country surround a question such as we are discussing, differ so greatly from those which would obtain in Great Britain. In the mother country, if an imputation went abroad that anything was wrong in the administration of justice all political parties would put their heads together and a full and thorough investigation had. And when, in his speech this afternoon the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) expressed surprise that Bill Miner has escaped in August, 1907, and that not until this late date was the matter brought up in the House of Commons, perhaps the explanation of that is that the members of the administration now in power in Canada do not relish full and proper criticism of their departments, and when it is borne in mind that until last October there was a solid phalanx of government supporters from British Columbia it is not surprising that the matter has not been brought to the attention of parliament until the present day. It is certainly not the custom with this government to allow its supporters to bring up for discussion matters which are calculated to embarrass or to annoy them. The Department of Justice is the most important department of government. We can afford mal-administra-tion in other departments; we are less than 7,000,000 of people occupying a country which can bountifully supply a population of one hundred millions; we are rich in natural resources and the appropriation of even hundreds of square miles of coal areas without adequate compensation to the country, and the exploitation of our forest resources by friends of the government, and the uncompensated depletion of our fisheries to supply the markets of the United States' cities are not so grievous after all because we have still enough left and to spare for our own supply. But, when it comes to the Department of Justice, that bulwark which stands between the citizens of Canada and all attacks on their liberties and rights, that department should be as Caesar's wife above suspicion. It is the duty of the Justice Department to investigate in the fullest manner anything that is calculated to reflect upon its administration, and even though the cloud hanging over it be but the size of a man's hand, it is incumbent on that department to endeavour to dispel it. Whether it be based on idle rumour or whether it be based on common gossip there is no doubt that suspicion has seized hold of the mind of the people with regard to the escape of the convict Bill Miner. The facts are briefly these: In 1906 the Canadian Pacific Railway as common carriers took charge of £50,000 of bonds to convey across this continent. The train

was held up at Mission Station on the Canadian Pacific Railway and was looted, and rumour had it that these £50,000 of bonds were stolen. Subsequently another train robbery took place and afterwards Bill Miner and his accomplices were arrested. It was to the credit of the administration of justice in Canada that he was tried, sentenced to a life term and incarcerated in the penitentiary at New Westminster. Now, rumour further says that the detectives of the Canadian Pacific Railway discovered that Bill Miner was the man who appropriated these £50,000 of bonds in 1906, and reasoning as ordinary men would they said: If we can approach this life term convict and get him to surrender these bonds or tell where they are concealed we will have accomplished a meritorious act. And so, one of the Canadian Pacific Railway detectives visited the penitentiary as also did a detective from the United States, and an ex fellon was taken in with Mr. Bullick and Bill Miner was interviewed in the penitentiary. Now, rumour further has it that when the proposition was put to Miner he answered: If I were out of here I could locate the bonds, and so arrangements were quietly made by which he left the penitentiary. It is further said that before his alleged escape his hair and hi3 moustache were allowed to grow, and while the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General have told the House that his hair did not exceed three-quarter inches in length, there appears to be no positive statement from these hon. gentlemen with regard to the moustache. At all events the statement is made that Miner was enabled to step without the penitentiary and to hand over these bonds to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) paid the Minister of Justice a flattering compliment; he spoke in glowing terms of the high position held by that hon. gentleman at the Bar, and I have pleasure in agreeing with everything that has been said as to the legal attainments of the distinguished gentleman whq is Minister of Justice. But Sir, the Minister of Justice paid small credit to that intelligence when, after telling us how he investigated the matter, he asked us: What more could I do? I submit that the ordinary business man, with the facts as rumour and gossip have placed them before the country, to take no more reliable source, would have worked on the conclusion back to Bill Miner. He would have found whether or not it was a fact that £50,000 of bonds were transported across this continent, whether these bonds had been stolen in transmission, and whether they had been restored. If these facts had been established, and if the telegram which Mr. Bourke said he sent to Mr. Dawson as inspector was changed, it is to be borne in mind that it came to Ottawa over ' Mr. MADDIN.
the wires of the Canadian Pacific Railway Coippa-ny, and if it was the object of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to compass the discharge of this man from the penitentiary in consideration of the return to them of the bonds, it would easily be a part of the scheme that any telegram sent to the Department of Justice over their wires would be intercepted.
Some hon. members have found fault with the hon. member who initiated this discussion this afternoon. That hon. member read from the Vancouver 'Province,' a paper which he said was independent and was published by reliable people, an imputation in heavy black type on the editorial page against the Department of Justice. I submit that an act of so grave a character as is involved in this case, which is nothing more or less in substance than an effort to usurp the pardoning power of the Crown, is something to be reprobated by both sides of this House. I regret that it is not viewed in that light by the members of the government, and that the Minister of Justice does not take it upon himself to investigate this matter to the fullest extent. As the party organ in Ottawa says, he has nothing to lose by doing so. If I drew the attention of the Postmaster General to a charge of dishonest conduct amongst the officials of the post office in Ottawa, and I told him that it came from a reliable source which I was not in a position to divulge, and if he took the matter up and discovered that something was wrong, it would be no reproach upon him or his administration. But if he hesitated or refused to investigate the matter, then I would say it was a reproach upon him- that he became a party to it. The Minister of Justice has pointed out that in all cases except those of capital offences, when pardon was sought, it was granted on the advice of the Minister of Justice. The Minister of Justice is a man above reproach, and I would not for one moment connect his name with this so-called conspiracy; but I do wish to point out that unless he takes the matter up and investigates it, there will be a lack of confidence in his department. The hon. minister pointed out that in the Brothier case this pardoning power was exercised by the Governor General on the recommendation of the Minister of Justice. Seemingly this could not be compassed by those who wished to get Bill Miner outside, and the conspiracy which is talked about did not extend to the heads of the department at Ottawa, but was fully worked among the officials of the penitentiary at New Westminster, with the result that Miner was permitted to escape.
Now, the path of duty in this case is quite clear. It becomes the duty of the Minister of Justice, under all the circumstances, to institute proceedings, to find out to what extent there is truth in the

statement that those bonds were stolen and that they have been restored, and if it be a fact that those bonds were stolen by Miner and restored by him, I think there is such a case of circumstantial evidence to submit to any jury that they would not be slow in finding that there was a conspiracy between the officials of the penitentiary and the friends of Miner on the outside.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton).
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I congratulate my hon. friend from South Cape Breton (Mr. Maddin) on the very eloquent manner in which he has presented his views to the House. My hon. friend is not without experience in the courts of this country or without knowledge of what is evidence and what is not evidence. My hon. friend speaks as if there had been no investigation of this matter at all. If the circumstances of the case, as presented from both sides of the House, had been without investigation up to this time, we would all say at once that certainly there should be an investigation. I do not know the terms of the Penitentiary Act in respect to discipline or in respect to investigations into matters of this kind; but it has been stated to-day by gentlemen who know, that that Act provides for an investigation in cases of this kind by the inspector. If that be the case, I take for granted that an investigation of such a character has taken place in this instance; and, if so, it has the same force as an investigation before a judge, because the officer is constituted a judge in such cases by the Act. Therefore it is no light matter to set aside as of no consequence the findings of that official. If my hon. friend would reverse the order of things and would say that gentlemen on the opposition side were content with what had been done by the inspector, and the Minister of Justice were coming here and asking for the consent of this House to a re-opening of the investigation, I can well imagine the storm with which he would be met, particularly by my hon. friend from South Cape Breton, to produce the evidence on which he based his request. Where is the evidence in this case? The opposition in this House is led by a distinguished lawyer, and there are a good many other lawyers in the opposition, and they speak with great flippancy of evidence. Where is the evidence? There are rumours in newspapers; are they evidence? If the hon. gentleman presented himself before any judge of this country to ask for a new trial of a case that had been tried, and the judge asked him, where is your new evidence, and my hon. friend would say, I have not a word of new evidence, but a certain newspaper publishes rumous that a certain official in a certain place said that if he were questioned he would tell something; would any judge or court allow the case to be re-opened? The judge would certainly tell him that he had no grounds on which to base any such application, and it would be summarily refused. That is the position here. An investigation has been held, every man who had anything to do with the penitentiary has been examined and there is not a particle of evidence, as far as appears here-there may be when the papers are brought down-that will connect Bourke or any other official of the penitentiary with aiding and abetting this man in his escape. But so far there is no such evidence, and I think it only fair to conclude that a proper investigation has taken place, and we must conclude that a proper decision has been reached, that nothing wrong has been found against the management of that penitentiary, except what has already been corrected by the suspension or dismissal of the acting warden and by the dismissal of some officials of the penitentiary.
What does the hon. member say about the well-established fact that the inspector who made the investigation is himself accused of having allowed surreptitious visits to be made to this man?

The superintendent or warden of the penitentiary has been examined on oath and we must assume he was properly examined, that every fact that could be elicited from him and every thing he knew was declared before the officer of the law who heard that evidence. He has been asked since the appearance of this newspaper story whether he had anything further to say. Does it make any difference what style of language was used in asking him if he had anything further to declare to his country in respect to the escape of these men? His reply was read here this afternoon, that he had nothing further to say. My answer to my hon. friend is that when a man declares upon his oath that he has fully and freely disclosed everything he knows about a certain fact, and he is asked afterwards, if there is anything in the rumours abroad that he has anything further to say and in reply to that inquiry he says: No, there is no truth in it, I have told you already on oath all I know of this matter, therefore it is quite unnecessary, in my judgment, to call upon him to give any further evidence

The Minister of Justice in answer to questions stated that surreptitious visits had been made with the consent of this very inspector to Miner before he escaped. Does it not occur to my hon. friend that this was not the right kind of inspector to pass judgment ?
I know of no evidence to that effect.
The Minister of Justice said that.
Did he say that ?

I did not understand that there was any alleged conspiracy between the officer who held the inquiry and any person in connection with the investigation. If there is I will ask my hon. friend to produce it or an evidence of it.

I do not produce it in the shape of using the word 'conspiracy.' I pointed out that the Minister of Justice said in answer to questions that a number of visits had been made improperly and that they should only be made with the consent of the inspector.

The Minister of Justice did not make the statement attributed to him, and if the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) will look at ' Hansard,' page 1227, where the whole statement of facts from the Justice Department is contained, he will find a direct denial of that statement.
Is that to-day's ' Hansard ' printed already ? I heard the Minister of Justice say it to-day.
He did not make the statement to-day either.

I have followed the answers of the Minister of Justice with a great deal of care and I am satisfied the position I took here is perfectly clear, that nothing of a wrong character has been brought home to the official who held the investigation. There was nothing that would disqualify him in my judgment or that should disqualify him in the judgment of this House or render him not a proper tribunal to try the charges in connection with that institution. Had there been, I certainly would not place any weight or base any argument on the investigation which he held. But I submit again that this investigation having been held there is nothing here presented that would justify us in asking the case to be reopened and a new trial to be held-and I submit that this investigation is more important than many a new trial would be.
I fully agree with the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Maddin) that it is a deplorable fact that party strife or squabbles should take place in this House or anywhere over the administration of justice. We are all proud of the administration of justice in Canada, we are proud of the respect which our people have for the law. It is one of our proud boasts, and

I am sure no person should attempt to make cheap political capital out of this matter even if a mistake had been made in connection with the administration of justice. The hon. gentleman who has just spoken said that the blame if blame there be does not come within a thousand miles of the Department of Justice or the learned gentleman who is to-day at the head of that department. That is the statement he has made. But supposing there was something wrong, there is tiot contention that the Department of Justice is in the slightest way implicated. It is said that officials of the penitentiary in British Columbia should not be called upon to do anything towards the capture of this individual. Miner, until they had instructions from Ottawa. I think that is a very unfair assumption to make, and it is dangerous to have a report go abroad from this House, that all we expect officials to do is to sit down and do nothing until directed from Ottawa. I take it that very much the same relationship exists between the Minister of Justice and the officials of the penitentiary as exist between the Attorney General of a province and the jailer or sheriff of a county. What would you think of a jailer or sheriff of. any county in Ontario who would sit down and twirl his thumbs if a prisoner es caped from a jail until he heard from the Utorney General of Ontario or got his directions ? We have a right to suppose that every penitentiary is well equipped with officers and that they have men to act in emergencies. Why should there be any necessity for communicating with Ottawa in order to capture this man? There were officers on the spot whose duty it was to take immediate action, and the officials of the penitentiary had at their beck and call all the resources of the government of British Columbia, who are interested equally with the government of Canada in the administration of justice. Therefore there is no point in saying that some time may have elapsed between the sending of the telegram and its receipt here. I submit there is not a particle of evidence upon which to base a further inquiry. We on the government side, as far as I know, have nothing to conceal. If any gentleman has evidence of a reliable and substantial character to lay before the government or the Minister of Justice, let us have it.
And, after that is done, if the Minister of Justice will not act upon it, there is some ground for fault finding. But, until that is done, I submit, an investigation having been held, the department is satisfied, and the Hr use, I think, should be satisfied, too, that everything has been done to ferret out the truth, and this question should not be made a means of gaining party advantage. The hdn. member for South Cape Breton
