(Mr. Maddin) declared that this should not be made a party question. He is a fairly regular attendant in this House, and knows how the party spirit was imported into the question. He knows that this was made a party question by his friend from New Westminster (Mr. J. D. Taylor) when the Solicitor General (Mr. Bureau) was putting his estimates through this House ten or twelve days ago. The hon. member from New Westminster knows that it is not a difficult matter to stir up party feeling in a body such as this House where the party lines are clearly marked. It is said that in the west there is a breezy honesty and sense of fair play. I am glad to know it. But I must say that I have not discovered any extreme measure of it in the hon. gentleman who has been bringing up this question from day to day. It is a well-known principle of British justice that no man may be attacked in our courts without giving him some notice of what is to be charged against him. I can tell my hon. friend from New Westminster that it is not fair to attack a man without giving him intimation so that he may have an opportunity to answer. We are told that the administration of justice outside this House must be extremely pure. I do not know that there is one kind of justice outside this House and another inside this House. I submit that if the reputation of a man is valuable outside this House, it is equally worthy of defence here. I submit also that if a man would be laughed out of court for presenting a case based upon an old newspaper and on a humdrum story and using this means to taking away the reputation of another man, he should be all the more laughed out of this House when he attacks the reputation of a minister of the Crown and a department of government on such evidence. The hon. member for South Cape Breton said that if a matter of this kind arose in England in connection with the Department of Justice, hon. gentlemen on both sides would get together and quiet1 inquire into the matter. We have strong men on both sides of this House. We have a competent lawyer leading the opposition, and we have a competent Minister of Justice. There should be no difficulty, according to the rule laid down by my hon. friend, for these two gentlemen to get together and quietly discuss this matter and find out if there is anything to investigate. I am sure that if the leader of the opposition would, in this quiet way, convince the Minister of Justice that there was something wrong, there would be no difficulty in getting an inquiry. But I submit, without impugning the motives of any person, that this would not suit the purpose at all. This could not get flaring headlines in the papers of Nova Scotia; we could not have the Jekyll and Hyde act in the newspapers and in this House if this quiet way were adopted. It suits the purpose very much better to carry
on the talk that we have heard. We have not been allowed to wait even until the papers come down. If the papers were down and we had the facts before us, possibly it would be [found that there was nothing to talk about. The great thing is to make a great hullabaloo about the matter and work up a lot of newspaper notoriety, get the matter before the public regardless of considerations of fairness; and hoping it will have some injurious effect upon the administration of justice and upon this government generally. My hon. friend from South Cape Breton knows very well the trick of the jury lawyer who tells his story to the judge: 'I want to prove so and so; I want to get in such and such evidence.' He knows that the judge will tell him that he cannot get in that evidence, but his object in telling the story is that the jury may hear it, and, no matter whether the judge admits it or not, the story will have more or less effect upon the minds of the men in the jury box. That is the scheme of these gentlemen-to get this story before the public right or wrong,- truth or falsehood does not make so much difference, so long as the story may have some effect on the jury and make a little cheap political capital.

Unfortunately I am not a lawyer, as are many of the gentlemen who have discussed this question, but, as this is a question relating to the west, I may be forgiven if I say a few words upon it. I shall not take up time in discussing the legal points involved. But, in fairness to the hon. member from New Westminster, I take exception publicly to the usage that the hon. gentleman (Mr. J. D. Taylor) received at the hands of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth). The Minister of Justice arraigned the hon. member for New Westminster on the strength of some articles that appeared in a paper published in British Columbia. The hon. member for New Westminster rose in his place and corrected the minister, yet the Minister of Justice did not have the'justice to acknowledge

'decency' is the word suggested by a friend beside me, did not have the decency to acknowledge-the fact that he had made a mistake. An apology was due from the Minister of Justice to my hon. friend from New Westminster. But the minister did not offer it. I hope the hon. minister will think again, and, later on, will tender to the hon. member for New Westminster the apology he owes him. The right hon. First Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) took it upon himself also to reprimand the hon. member for New Westminster. It was a reprimand worded as such a reprimand can be worded by only one man in this House-the Prime Minister himself-in the most courteous terms possible. It showed the steel hand in the

velvet glove. But even such a reprimand was not due from the First Minister of the great Dominion to a new member of this House. The First Minister accused the hon. member of discourtesy to one of the ministers in not officially notifying him that this discussion would be brought up. He left the impression that a rule of the House had been broken by my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. Taylor). I want to tell him and to tell this House through you, that no rule of this House was broken, there is no rule of ^ that _ kind. If the First Minister wants to shield himself by any supposed rule of that kind, let him amend the rules of the House and provide that when a discussion of this kind comes on notification must be given. There was no notification necessary, because the last few weeks this matter has been a live question in the House. It was brought before the Solicitor General on the 11th of JFebru-ary last, and he showed on that occasion that there was one Bureau at least in the government of Canada where one could apply for information and not get it. Therefore I say the question is not new, it was something that the Department of Justice already had in hand. A motion had been passed by this House at the instance of the hon. member for New Westminster, calling for the papers pertaining to this inquiry to be laid on the table. That motion was passed over two weeks ago, and yet the Solicitor General to-night stated, through the mouth of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) that there was no motion for papers. Why, Sir, he cannot be attending to his business, because it is his duty as Solicitor General to prepare those papers when they are asked for by the House.
I was somewhat surprised to hear the defence which the hon. member for Pictou made of the Minister of Justice. He told this House that the Minister of Justice was the greatest lawyer in Canada, the finest lawyer in Canada. Well, Sir, if beclouding the real facts of the case by a display of verbosity constitutes a great lawyer, then I want to tell the hon. member for Pictou that I absolutely agree with him; but if that is the duty of the greatest and finest lawyer in Canada, I have only to say that thanks be, I am only an old farmer. The hon. member for Pictou found fault with the members on this side of the House discussing this great issue before the papers that were called for had been brought down. I suppose he acts on the old axiom that the exception proves the rule, and therefore he went to work to discuss the question himself. But in his discussion of the question he showed, I think, in the opinion, not only of the members on this side of the House, but in the opinion of the members on the other side, that if any man in the House had no right to get up and discuss this question it was the hon. mem-Mr. CAMPBELL.
ber for Pictou himself, because he showed absolute ignorance of it. Let me point out to that hon. gentleman that in future when he desires to, discuss a question that is brought up in this House, it would be well for him to be in his place looking after the interests of his constituents, instead of running round the country doing all the mischief he can. The very fact that the hon. member for Pictou was called upon to deliver the speech he did to-night shows conclusively that he was called in as a forlorn hope. He has always been called upon as the leader of a forlorn hope, in committees and everywhere else, the last two sessions.
I hope this House will take his remarks at their true value, and take that particular matter into its consideration.
I do not intend to speak at length on this question, as it is one relating to a criminal matter that is foreign to me. My only object in rising is to pour oil on the troubled waters. The facts, as I understand them, are these: This man Miner was captured, tried and sentenced to the penitentiary for life, for one of the gravest crimes that had ever been perpetrated in Canada. After being incarcerated for a certain length of time, he escaped. An investigation was held, and as a result of that investigation, one of the minor officials was fired, or perhaps I should say suspended, for since then he has been taken back to work. Another man, as the hon. member for Pictou improperly said, was suspended, or was asked to send in his resignation. I said ' improperly,' and I use the word advisedly. This man was not asked to send in his resignation, he sent it in of his own accord. He asks for superannuation and gets it. Nobody has been punished, among the officials of the penitentiary at New Westminster, for inefficiency and neglect of duty. Nobody in this country, whether Liberal or Conservative, doubts for one moment but that some one was to blame. If any member of this House, in the conduct of his private business, finds an employee to blame, he punishes that individual. It is up to the government, it is up to the Department of Justice, to punish some one in regard to this matter, because the worst criminal that Canada has had in the clutches of the law for the last decade, has escaped, and nobody has been punished. The government supporters are handing put boquets to every official who could be biamed. The man who -was in charge, this man Bourke, was allowed to resign and got his full pension; the government did for him all that it could do to any man who had performed his duty with the utmost fidelity.	_	_
Now what are we asking on this side of the House, and what every decent man in Canada ought to be asking is: that the truth shall be made known. An investigation was held and held by an official who

is the object of a certain degree of public suspicion, who held the investigation himself, who tried his own case and who was practically his own judge and jury. That investigation has resulted in nothing, looking at it from the standpoint of justice. Certain things have come out since. There are rumours possibly but there never was smoke without fire. Certain rumours have come out. There is more perhaps than mere rumour. The deputy warden, who was allowed to retire and who was superannuated as if he were the finest official in the service of the government, has come out in different papers over his own name with a specific statement, amounting almost to a charge, to the effect that if he were brought before an impartial tribunal he would give evidence which has never been adduced and would do something to clear the atmosphere in this regard. It has been proved that the hole in or under the wall, through which this man Miner was supposed to have escaped, would not have accommodated a man of his size, and that it was absolutely impossible for him to have made his escape in that way. It has come out further that this man Miner has been permitted against the law, that is administered by the Minister of Justice, to grow a moustache-somebody said whiskers-and also hair to the length of three-quarters of an inch in a limited time. Three-quarters of an inch is a respectable growth of hair particularly on the top of the head, and I will submit to the judgment of the hon. Solicitor General upon that point.
What about the Minister of Justice?

I would tell my hon. friend that in my youth I was taught to respect gray hairs and even if the gray hairs are not on the top of the head I still have to respect the hon. Minister of Justice, and therefore I shall not refer to them. But those are facts that have been brought out since this so-called investigation was held. On this side of the House we take no exception to what was brought out at that previous investigation, but what we say is that the points that I have brought forward were not disclosed at that investigation and that all western Canada, and British Columbia particularly, believes that there was some collusion or that the intervention of influential corporations or parties, led to the letting out of this man Miner. These points have been brought' out, but they were not brought out at the investigation, and we ask the government to give us an investigation, or some kind of independent tribunal, that' will go into these matters and see whether or not there is any truth in them. On behalf of the government themselves I appeal to them to adopt this course. I want to tell the right hon.
Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) that the suspicion is all over Canada to-day that there is something crooked in this matter, and on behalf of the Canadian people and also on behalf of the great Liberal party, it is up to him to insist on having a free, independent tribunal that will bring Bourke before them and will not only bring Bourke before them but will bring one of these three convicts who escaped along with Miner and who has since been recaptured, as I heard it stated in the House, and who will give evidence to show how he got out and whether there was any collusion. We only ask it in the spirit of fair play. We only ask it to clear and not to damn the fair name of the Minister of Justice. We want the minister to have his name as clean as it ought to be and as I believe it would be did he give us this investigation. I have here, sir, if it will be any benefit' to the House, a picture of Bill Miner. I understood the other night that the Solicitor General said that about a month ago they had news of the whereabouts of Bill Miner? Am I right?
I beg your pardon.

I understood the Solicitor General, on the 11th February, sitting on the front benches, to say that he had news of the whereabouts of Bill Miner and expected to get him in a few days. Has he anything further in reference to that to communicate to the House?
I said I was informed that it was expected that they would capture him.

In closing I just want' to make this appeal, and I want to make it to the right hon. First Minister. We are not speaking here to-night, we have not done so to-day or upon any other occasion when the matter came up, for partisan purposes. We are all Canadians, whether we be Liberals or Conservatives. There is a blot of suspicion on the fair name of Canada, with reference to the administration of justice. It is a little matter, a matter of very little moment with regard to the question of expense, it would not cost much to appoint a committee, or whatever you like to call it, an independent tribunal, who will investigate, who will bring this man Bourke, who will bring this prisoner who was taken the other day before them, get from them whatever information can be got and clear up this business for ever and a day. It is only justice that we are asking.
Motion .agreed to and House went into Committee of Supply.
Trent canal-Construction, $1,000,000.

As I understand it the appropriation for the work on the Holland river is included in this vote for the Trent

canal, although the former work has nothing to do with the Trent canal at all. 1 do not think those two votes should be put in a lump sum, but at all events we should have some information as to how much it is intended to expend on the Holland river.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext: In including these twu votes in the one appropriation we are following the precedent of last year. We will spend about $200,000 on the Holland division. I have stated that it would cost $600,000 but I believe that it will cost much more than that before it is completed.

I do not want to delay the passing of the estimates, but this is going to be a contentious matter and as there are several returns on the Order Paper with respect to it which have not yet been disposed of I would ask that this vote be deferred.
I do not think there is any return asked for, but there is a question on the Order Paper with regard to it.

And it was asked that that question should be put in the form of a return.
' Mr. GRAHAM. Perhaps I can give the information now.

I have asked for the following information by question number 8 on the Order Paper.
1.	How much money was spent on the Newmarket canal on the Holland river, before 31st March, 1908?
2.	How much money was spent in April, May, June, July, August, September, October, November and December of 1908?
3.	What contracts were let since 31st of March, 1908, and the amount of such contracts ?
4.	Were tenders asked for?
5.	Who are the contractors?

The Minister had ample time to answer this question before, but he asked for his convenience that it should be put in the form of a motion for a return and now he says he can give the information right away.
I did not ask that the question should be put in the form of a return.

There is a deeper principle than that involved. Here is an appropriation for $1,000,000 in which two independent and separate works are included. The Holland river is -30 miles away from the Trent canal, and yet we are asked to allow this vote to slide through without obtaining detailed information. We would not be doing our duty to* our constituents if wei did not learn how much is to be expended on the Holland river and Mr. WALLACE
how much on the Trent canal and where the work is to be done. If this vote goes through the Minister can spend the whole cne million dollars on the Holland river if he wishes to and not one cent on the Trent canal. It is a reasonable request to ask that this item should stand until we get the information which will enable us to discuss it in an intelligent way.

While my hon. friends here are directly interested in this matter I have a general interest in it, and early in the session I asked for the complete papers as I wanted if possible to find out whatever in the world set this Holland river work going at first and what were the representations that ever induced a sane department to undertake to build the Newmarket canal. I have not obtained that information, and if the government is going to spend a lot of money on that work we ought to know something about it. The minister will make more progress if he allows this vote to stand till we get full information.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not know whether I can give any information as to the manner in which this work came to be undertaken, but I can at least disclaim any right to the honour that the hon. member for North Ontario sought to do me the other evening when he said it was the custom in that part of the country to couple my name with this work. That was a piece of new s to me, as I imagine it was to everybody who heard it. I think it was a compliment. I should be very proud indeed to have my name connected with any public work in the constituency of North York which the people of that constituency took an interest in or that was for the welfare of the community. But I do not want to sail under false colours. I do not claim any credit for this undertaking; I have never done so, either in this House or out of it, for the simple reason that I had nothing whatever to, do with it, and have no right to take any credit for it. I entered this house, as hon. gentlemen mostly know, in the fall of 1905. At that time there had been a vote of $100,000 passed by this parliament in the previous session. I have always understood that the way in which that vote came to be passed was that a very numerous and very important delegation of the principal men of the county of North York came to Ottawa during the spring of 1905 and made representations to the government and to the Minister of Railways and Canals, as the result of which it was determined to undertake this work.
I have lying before me a list of names of some of those who came specially from North York at that time for the purpose of urging their views upon the government. In that list are such well known names as those of Mr. T. H. Lennox, M.P.P., the pre-

sent member for North York in the legislature of Ontario; Mr. F. W. Daville, who has since then been made sheriff of the county of York; Mr. T. H. Brunton, a well known member of the Conservative party, I think at that time and probably still president of the association for the riding; Mr. Archibald McCallum, who was at that time I think reeve of the township of King, who was the gentleman I had the honour of opposing at the by-election in the fall of 1905, a man of the highest standing in the community, and a man whom I need not Bay I hold personally in the highest esteem and respect; Mr. A. McMurchy, a member of the township council of King and also a leading Conservative of the county; and I might go on to give other names simply to show that there was absolutely nothing political, and not the slighest thought of politics, in the matter. This was literally the body of the county of North York, whatever that might be worth, and it was just as much a Conservative undertaking as it was a Liberal undertaking. Everybody in North York knows that, and I should welcome the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. S. Sharpe) if he would now or at any time pay a visit to the riding of North York, and make any attack upon this undertaking or upon the men who initiated it and believed that it was for the good of Canada. I certainly should not ask for any better assistance towards that waning of political influence which the hon. gentleman attributed to me when he was addressing this committee last week, and which he said was due to the fact that I had originated or advocated this scheme. Let that political influence continue to wane if my hon. friend's efforts to identify me with it has anything to do with accelerating it towards the vanishing point. I can only assure him that the more opposition he will offer to the construction of that canal, in that locality, the more he will feed the popularity of the man who has the honour to represent that constituency at the present time. That of course is but natural. I suppose that whenever any public work is desired in any locality, the men who live there, and who think it will be for the benefit of the business centres of the locality, unitedly and generally, favour it, with regard to political considerations. I think that the hon. member for North Ontario would not object to the construction of the public building in his own home town of Uxbridge, for which there is a vote in the estimates. I think he would be very glad to take it, and I am quite sure that the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) has on more than one occasion in this House urged the building of a branch of this very Newmarket canal up to the village or town of Bradford, a few miles to one side in his constituency. The very deputation which came here orig-60

mating this scheme and urging it upon the government contained representatives of his constituents-I know nothing of their politics-from the town of Bradford and the township of West Gwillimbury; and because they thought they would be served by the construction of the branch which the hon. member from South Simcoe has advocated in this House, they were in favour of this work and united in urging it on the government of that day. But without any reference to what the origin of this work was, the question before this committee is whether or not public money should be voted towards carrying it on, and I want to address myself very briefly to that question. Some $200,000 or $300,000, I suppose, has already been put into the work. Now, if no more money is to be voted for it, it stands uncompleted and the country loses the money that has been put into it. I fully admit that if the work will be absolutely valueless, if it was abject folly to have undertaken it, the best thing we can do is to abandon it, notwithstanding what has been done by the people who came here clamouring for it, and by the people here who were weak enough to yield to that clamour and to undertake the work for them. It was not this parliament, it was not your humble servant who now addresses you, who had anything to do with it. It was our predecessors, and I am by no means prepared to say that they made any kind of mistake in doing what they did. A good deal of fun has been poked at this enterprise by the newspapers. I have not the slightest objection to that. I have enjoyed as much as anybody a great many cartoons that I have seen about it in which I figure. I do not any the less enjoy a good joke because it is at my expense, and I have no objection to the cartoonists exercising their art with me as a subject if they think it of any consequence to do so. But if it comes to be a serious question in this House, and if hon. gentlemen here seriously present for consideration to the committee the contention that this canal, when it is finished to Newmarket, will not have water wherewith to float any boat or be of any practical service to this country, that is another story altogether ; and it is seriously that I want to say a few words with reference to this undertaking, assuming that any one who criticises it or thinks it cannot become a valuable means of transportation to Newmarket and to the adjoining villages, is dealing with the subject in equal seriousness.
This is no question of law, it is not one upon which I am in the least degree competent to form an opinion for myself. If it were a legal question and I had any strong view about the law of the matter I would be prepared to back that view at any rate as far as the Privy Council, before I would come to the conclusion that I had been

wrong. It is not that kind of a question. Being a purely engineering problem, I am not competent to deal with it, but I am prepared to place exactly the same confidence in the opinion of a distinguished engineer, that I am egotistical enough, if you like, to say I would place in my own opinion if it were a matter of law. I have known the gentleman who is now the deputy minister and chief engineer of the Department of Railways and Canals since he and I were boys side by side on the shores of the Bay of Quinte. I have seen him rise higher and higher in his chosen profession until to-day I believe there is no man in the Dominion of Canada who stands higher as an engineer than he; and having in his engineering opinion as absolute confidence as I honestly think he would have in my opinion upon a purely legal question, I am prepared to rest my satisfaction with the proposition to construct this work upon his opinion as a matter of engineering, that there is ample water supply for all the working purposes of that canal when it has been constructed.
When was that opinion given?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Butler's opinion has been given to me in private conversation on more than one occasion. I have asked him if he had any doubt about it, but he says he has none upon the information he has received of the surveys. I am not competent to go into the figures or test at all the correctness of his view.
When was that opinion given, and was it put on paper?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As recently as this afternoon. I asked him this afternoon if there was any question about it in his mind. It was never put on paper to me, he and I are too well acquainted to deal with each other on the footing of a piece of paper. I rest my confidence in the practicability of this work upon the opinion of the gentleman to whom I have referred. If other members of the House have not the same confidence in him, that is a matter in regard to which each must form his own opinion.
Was the opinion of the deputy minister based on personal inspection or on the reports of other engineers?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend will have to obtain that information from the department. I am not able to tell him whether Mr. Butler has made a personal inspection or not. I asked him on the subject as an old friend, and as the man in charge of that department of the public service, and because of these repeated gibes or jokes about the great waterless canal that the country was building. I am of course, discussing it altogether on the Mr. AYLESWORTH.
supposition that this is not an impracticable work, not a work that will have no water wherewith to float a barge after the canal is completed. If I am wrong in that supposition I quite agree with hon. gentlemen that the work should be stopped. No one will propose seriously to construct a ditch to serve as a canal that will have no water after it is finished. It seems to me we ought seriously to consider whether or not this undertaking, supposing it to be practicable, is for the benefit of the country to the extent of the amount of money that will be put into it. As to that, let me remind hon. gentlemen who represent that part of the country-I think I see pretty nearly all of them opposite me, I think I have the honour to occupy an oasis of fertile territory surrounded by a vast desert of Conservative, shall I sav of unfertile country-let me remind these gentlemen who represent that part of Ontario, of the departed glories of Holland Landing and Holland river. Long before I had any acquaintance with that part of Ontario, Holland Landing received its name. How did it get it? How else than that it had its wharf, its landing place, and was the port for Lake Simcoe? In the old days before the advent of railways, barges and scows, I do not know of what draught, but vessels of some kind or other, were continually brought up the Holland river as far as Holland Landing. They used the landing for commercial purposes of transport, and although that village has now the air very much of a deserted village, I admit, it shows, in the buildings which still remain and the works or their remnants along the river, evidence of the prosperity that once visited it when it was literally one of the lake ports of Ontario. If traffic by water was possible, as it undoubtedly was a hundred years ago or fifty years ago, prior to the construction of railways, if it were profitable to navigate the river from Lake Simcoe as far as Holland Landing, why would that navigation not be profitable again if the silt and sand which in course of time has filled up that stream below Holland Landing is removed? The first half of the work which this vote proposes to provide for was the cleaning out of the natural bed, the straightening of it in places and the making of that river once more navigable as far to the south of Lake Simcoe or Cook's bay as Holland Landing. That was the head of navigation naturally and up that far boats could now go if there was a dredging and deepening of the natural stream and all the better if there were a straightening of the river where it was too winding- in its course. That is the first branch of the work that was undertaken in section 1, I think, of the Newmarket or Holland River division of this canal. And no one, I say, could successfully contend that there is not ample water for navigation purposes in that part of the stream.

What is the condition above it? Newmarket is the principal town in the constituen cy, and has a population, I suppose, of 4,000 or 5,000 people. It is some three miles- possibly not more than two and one-half miles by direct route-further up the natur al stream than Holland Landing. The stream would not be navigable for any economical purpose any further up than Holland Landing so long as it remains in a state of nature. At Newmarket there is already a dam thrown across the stream, and a pond in consequence created. I do not know how many feet in depth that pond may be, but the dam, I should say, from personal observation, must be twenty-five or thirty feet high. I suppose there is at least that volume of water behind it, covering perhaps some eight or ten'acres in the present pond, and this, without any attempt at conservation, storage or utilizing to best advantage the water which by nature will come to that water-course or stream. I am not pretending to argue whether or not it is practicable, I only know that any one who passes up and down alonv the railway or drives about Newmarket can see these things for himself. And, if engineers, having made their survey, report to us, and if the deputy minister and chief engin eer of the department, upon his responsibility as head officer of that department tells us that it is in his judgment a practicable work, I am content, I am prepared to take the responsibility of voting public money for the doing of this work upon his confidence that it is a perfectly practicable scheme. The building of this canal from Holland Landing to Newmarket is, of course, not a dredging operation, it is the ordinary construction of a canal, which will replace the natural stream which now runs from Newmarket to Holland Landing. As to the commercial value of the work when it is comnleted, I entertain no kind of doubt. Newmarket is to-day as great a business centre as many of the towns along the line of any of our canals, a larger place than many of the towns on the St. Lawrence canals, than many of the towns along the line of the Trent canal, than many of the towns along the line of the Welland canal, a place of at least equal importance, I should sav with the county town of Lincoln, with which the hon. member (Mr. Lancaster) from that constituency is well acquainted. The Welland canal, of course, a great national undertaking for through traffic between the lakes, is not to be compared to something of local concern such as this either in the expenditure it involves to the country or in its importance to the country once it comes to be constructed. But my contention with regard to this canal is simply this, that just as anv other public work into which you might 601
put an equal amount of mone" is for the benefit of that locality primarily, so this public work, once it is completed, will be very greatlv to the benefit of the riding of North York and the adjoining riding of South Simcoe. The Holland river is the boundary between the township of East Gwillimbury which belongs to North York and West Gwillimbury, which belongs to South Simcoe, and each of these townships and the locality generally will reap the advantage of this canal when it comes to be completed. With regard to the advantage of it to the people there, I venture to say to the hon. gentlemen who are criticising it, hon. gentlemen representing the adjoining constituencies, that there are, in the riding of North York at all events, no two opinions. I have not at any time made the construction of this canal a political question in that constituency. It would be idle for me to attempt to do so because the people there know equally well with myself-in fact, much better than I do-how that work came to be initiated. They have heard and seen in the newspapers periodical attacks upon this work, attacks to which, I have always thought, the city of Toronto contributed, possibly, more than any other portion of the province. Although Newmarket, as compared with the city of Toronto, is a small place, it is not without the usual local jealousy. There is already, and has been for years, an agitation in the north end of the county of York for separation, a desire to set up a separate county for themselves, with Newmarket as the county town. There have been continual attacks, I may say. from the public platform upon this undertaking on the part of members of this House from the city of Toronto. The hon member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) it seemed to me, could scarcely make a platform speech without denouncing the horrible outrage of this waste of public money in the Newmarket canal. That is good politics for me in North York, I am willing to admit, but other than in that sense, there are no politics about it. On the public platform, on nomination day, last October, my opponent referred to my course during the last parliament as representing North York and asked what I had done for the constituency. He did not pretend to say: This man has brought us the canal. If he had done so, I suppose, he would have answered his own question. In that connection, upon that occasion, I said from the hustings that, while I had had nothing to do with it, and had never, so far as I was aware, asked for one dollar of expenditure in North York, I thought that those who attacked the expenditure upon this canal could be found, in every instance, among the ranks of our political opponents, and that those who defend it were, perhaps necessarily, upon the side of those who were

making the expenditure. But it was only in that sense that the question, so far as I nan see, had the least element of political significance in it. I remain entirely of this [DOT]opinion. That work never was of political significance, it was simply a piece of local work which the people of the locality, without regard to politics, united in wanting, and, so far as I know, unite in wanting still And, exactly as the inhabitants of any other town in the province would like to see public money expended in their midst, so the people of North York would be very much dissatisfied, I am sure, if anything were done to interfere with the completion of this work.

I think the Hon Minister of Justice (Mr. Ayles-worth) intended to leave the impression with the newer members of this House that the last parliament had been unanimous in voting a sum of money for this canal. I wish to say that the members on this side, when this was originally introduced, objected just as strongly as they do to-night, and that just as strong exception was taken by the members acquainted with the locality as on the present occasion.
Now we are told that the people from that riding, of both political stripes, came down here and petitioned the government to spend a sum of money on this canal in North York. Now I do not suppose there is any riding in Canada that will raise a strong objection to half a million of money being spent therein, whether it serves a useful purpose or otherwise; the people derive an immediate benefit from the expenditure. Now with regard to the canal itself, I took strong objection to it when the scheme was first proposed. A great deal was said with regard to the water supply. I thought then, and I think now, that it is of very little importance, because the canal will be just as useful dry as it will be wet. There is nothing to sail up or down it, so it is no concern of this parliament whether there is ever a drop of water to supply the canal or not. Now we are told there are institutions in North York that will benefit by this canal. I am somewhat familiar with the situation, and with some of the people there, and I know of no institution that will benefit to any appreciable extent, with the exception of one or two particular pets of this government. I believe there was another enterprise which was carried on a few years ago down on the Holland Flats, catching frogs. But I believe that enterprise has lapsed somewhat of late, and if this canal is constructed it will perhaps revive it. I do not know of any other good purpose that will be served by building the canal. Perhaps down in lower stretches towards Lake Sim-eoe, it may be partitioned off and the farmers along there may utilize it for rais-Mr. AYLESWORTH.
ing ducks or geese. Perhaps the upper stretches might be used for sheep pens, or pig pens, where the land is a little dryer. But I do not know of anything else that can be done with it.
Now, Sir, I take exception to the amount of money that is being sunk in an enterprise of this kind. I want to remind the minister, and I want to remind this committee, that it will not be only the original amount of money we put into it that this country will have to furnish, but there will be large sums required annually for the upkeep of this useless enterprise. The gates on the locks will rust on their hinges, and will have to be renewed from time to time. A large number of employees will have to be paid annually. We are loading upon the country, not [DOT] only the original sum, but an additional large sum yearly to keep up the appearance. In the riding I represent we have a good deal of navigation, and we have vainly appealed for the last two or three years to this government for some works that are badly needed there. Last year a small estimate was put through for a little wharf, 1 think somewhere about $4,000, but this year that is cut out altogether; on account of hard times the government can't afford to go on with it. I want to say here, realizing what I am saying, that in the town of Gravenhurst, where this little grant was made for a wharf, there will be as much navigation in one year as there will be on this Holland river enterprise for all time to come. Now I want to put this thought particularly before the minister, that if this $200,000 or thereabouts that he proposes to put into that canal next summer, were spread over those northern waters where they need accommodation very badly, and where there is a number of steamers to land, he would be doins? a great deal of good to that northern country, opening up and developing it. But down there where there is nothing and never can be anything for a steamboat to do, this money will be wasted. I feel strongly on this matter, and I would ask the minister carefully to consider it. I want to say that when this vote was first introduced it was distinctly destined for this canal, and was not coupled up with any Trent Valley matter whatever. I do not know of any reason why the minister should mix up the Holland Eiver canal with the Trent Valley canal, unless it is to put us in the position that if we object to the one we should have to object to the other. I do not object to going on with the Trent Valley canal. I am not much enamoured with the enterprise, but it has been accepted by both sides of the House and it was commenced a great many years ago when the prospects were more promising than they are to-day. In any event, both sides of the House are committed to the Trent Valley project, and we must carry it through. But we are not commit-

ted to this Holland river enterprise, at least on the_ opposition side of the House. We have objected to it from the first, and I think the minister ought to deal with the two enterprises separately. Now the Minister of Justice thinks there is only one opinion in North York with regard to the enterprise. I heartily concur with him. I have talked with people in North York, and I have yet to find a single individual, man, woman or child, who thinks this enterprise will be of any use in North York outside the temporary expenditure of money in its construction. I think the minister would fail to find a single ratepayer in North York who would say, over his own signature, that this work will be of any benefit to the people after it is built. I will not say any more on the question at present. This matter will come up again, as the minister is going to make an announcement upon it, and I reserve any further remarks until then.

I wish to call the attention of the committee to the fact that the Minister of Justice has not given the history of this transaction exactly as it occurred. He was good enough to introduce my name, and that is one reason why I wish to say a word or two. I happened to be here at the time when this project was first broached in the House. Let me inform the committee that it originated in a meeting at Newmarket, at which Sir Wm. Mulock was present as the representative of that riding, the riding of North York, and that Sir Wm. Mulock was then an active promoter of the scheme. That all originated before the meeting of that deputation to which the hon. gentleman referred to-night. The enterprise, so far as I can ascertain by the records, was virtually originated by Sir Wm. Mulock. Sir Wm. Mulock was the father of the scheme, and made it a stepping stone in the election which was then pending. I made that charge on the 17th of February, and it was not denied. I referred to it as an election scheme. Sir Wm. Mulock had brought forward this scheme of deepening the creek between Newmarket and the Holland river, and expending a large sum of money. I referred to an article which appeared in the ' Witness,' and I said:
Let me read a word or two from the Bradford ' Witness,' which is a paper not altogether published in the interest of my hon. friend, but published in the riding lie formerly represented.
The article is dated February 9 and it is headed ' The Trent Valley canal extension
Our readers will remember that a public meeting was held in Newmarket last September to consider the advisability of steps being taken to deepen the east branch of the Holland river via Holland Landing, Newmarket and Aurora and the west branch to
Fchomberg, in order to make these waters available for commercial purposes in connection with the Trent Valley canal system which Bill shortly be continued to Lake Simcoe. Sir Wm. Mulock, the Hon. E. J. Davis, Mayor Kane, of Newmarket

Another good supporter of my hon. friend. -Mayor Daville, of Aurora, spoke in favour of the scheme

' Scheme ' is the very word.
-and a large committee was appointed to promote this great undertaking.
Was the Postmaster General (Sir Wm. Mulock) present at that meeting ?

He was the ohief spokesman in favour of this scheme to promote the general interest and prosperity of Canada through his own riding and through his own supporters. The hon. gentleman (Sir Wm. Mulock) seems to have been the ohief person on that occasion, as we would naturally ex pect him to be.
Since that meeting government engineers have made careful survey of the territory

Mark you, my hon. friend, the Minister of Justice tells us to-night that this scheme originated in a deputation coming down and waiting upon Sir William Mulock in the city of Ottawa, but I will point out to you, Mr. Chairman, that Sir William Mulock on this occasion, invites me to attend with the deputation.
It would need to be careful if it favours the putting through of this canal.
The Minister of Justice seemed to think that I used to be in favour of this scheme. I thank God I never was.
-and, although no official report has yet been made, it is pretty well understood that the engineers will report favourably upon the matter.
They have their instructions, in other words, I need not take up much time over the intervening part. I appreciate that it might be said that this newspaper item may not be correct. Surely it cannot be that the engineers were actually on the ground surveying it before the deputation came down at all. Let us see as to that. Turning over a few pages I find this:

The hon. gentleman is very funny.
That was referring to Sir William Mulock.
He tries to get away from the point. Does the hon. gentleman deny, as is stated in the paper, that he was present at the meeting and spoke in favour of the scheme? I read it, not only in the paper but I read it in other papers, amongst them the Newmarket 'Era,' 1 think.
The Newmarket ' Era ' was a liberal paper.
While I was travelling on the train I met a gentleman who had just come from the meeting. I know it was discussed broadcast

throughout the last general election, and 1 am calling attention to it here because I think it does not become a cabinet minister, on the ove of an election, to make promises to the electors which may influence their votes.

An abstract declaration of principle may be a very good thing. I attended the meeting in question, I addressed myself to the meeting as other citizens did, and I was saying what I am saying now, that the district would be advantaged by the construction of such a work, but the question of its cost and the question of its feasibility were matters entirely in the future, and the determination of the work must depend upon these considerations. That is ray view to-day. I hope the result of the inquiry will show that the work is feasible, and that the prices come within a reasonable figure or as reasonable as will commend itself to support at the hands of this House.

Is it a fact that engineers or surveyors were put on?
Sir William Mulock does not evidently want to answer that question because he says:
When we come to discuss that question, the way it happened to come up at that time will be made clear.
I assert here and now that the way that the matter happened to come up was that Kane Bros., the most influential men in the riding of Sir William Mulock, wanted it to promote their own industry, and that they were the originators of this scheme. Continuing Sir Wm. Mulock said:
It grew out of the decision of the Railway Commission seriously affecting a great enterprise in our district. The people were seriously intending to move away because of the railway freight rates. The matter came up in that way, and the people of our district were extremely uneasv lest this large enterprise should move away on account of the iates of freight charged by the Grand Trunk Railway Company on the commodities used and exported by that enterprise.
The hon. gentleman has not answered me, but probably he will tell me now ?
About the engineers?
Yes.

The engineers have been in the field ever since, and I think they are in the field yet.
Mr. LENNOX I do not want to prolong this matter; if the hon. gentleman will tell me now, that is an end of it-what large enterprise was it that was about to leave?
Messrs. Kane & Sons.
Of Newmarket?
Of Newmarket.
Yes, the gentleman who is named in this paper as the promoter of this scheme.
He is one of the firm.
By what authority were these engineers sent into the field?

By the authority of the Minister of Railways.
So we have it established as clear as anything can be established that this transaction originated in the way that it is here described. Then we go on and discuss the matter and Sir William Mulock tells me that a deputation is coming down within three or four days from the riding of North York; he understands that some of my own constituents will be here with that deputation and he invites me to attend it. I did go and listen as he had invited me. He said that I would be convinced, but I was not convinced, and I am not convinced yet. I think I will not be convinced as the time goes on because it has demonstrated more and more the utter uselessness and absurdity of the scheme. The Minister of Justice thought it was worth while to refer to the personnel of that deputation. I cannot say that I am surprised at the Minister of Justice. I have been here since 1905 when he came in and I am not a bit surprised that he thought it magnificent argument to put up, that T. Herbert Lennox, representative of the riding, at the request of people who wanted money expended in the riding, came down as one of the deputation. Where have we drifted since then? What was the amount that was said to be the total expenditure for the scheme ? I understood from some members of the deputation that it was then said that it would cost $350,000. What is it to cost now ? I do not know whether it was for the purpose of influencing votes during the last election, but it was reported during the election that there was going to be $.3,500,000 expended upon the work. The Minister of Justice has thought fit to refer to the fact that I have advocated the digging of a trench from the Holland river proper up to the railway station at Bradford. In that he is entirely mistaken. My constituents at Bradford have felt that inasmuch as the government carried away the wharf which they should have built in South Simcoe and put it across on the other side of the river so that they have to cross the river in order to get to the wharf which should serve them on Holland river, they were entitled to have a cutting made up to the railway station and they sent in a petition in regard to the matter. As representative of that riding I had the honour to present that petition, as I shall be happy to accede to any proper request which my constituents make to me. The hon. gentlemen will not find that I have advocated the scheme further than to represent the wishes of my constituents in that regard. But, there is a thousand miles of difference between that scheme of cutting a trench up to the railway station, if it can be done for a moderate expenditure, and this mad-cap scheme of

spending one million dollars or two million dollars for a cutting which has already demonstrated itself as an absolutely indefensible scheme. Last summer in going through _ that county * two or three times a week in the dry season-and I want to say that it was a particularly dry season last year and could not be taken as a fair average-but in going through that district last year I never could detect that any water was escaping beyond the pond or dam in the village of Newmarket. In other words, all the water of that stream appeared to be evaporating from the surface of the pond, and scores of people passing up and down noticed the same fact. This is an absolutely indefensible expenditure of public money and notwithstanding the fact that so much money has been squandered already on it I believe it would be wise at this point to stop.

The request of my hon friend to allow the item to stand until the return is brought down is a fair one and I
am ready to accept it.
Will the min ister divide the appropriation so that we will know the expenditure on the different parts- of the work?
I will tell my hon. friend approximately what will be expended on each.

It is not what
the minister purposes doing but what he will do when he gets the item through that we would like to know.
I hope my hon. friend does not mean that insinuation.
I did not intend to reflect on the minister and I do not want factious opposition to the item, but we surely should have that information.

I told my hon. friend the other night how the expenditure was to be divided, but I will make it more explicit when the vote comes up again. I also gave the reasons why the two were considered the one scheme.

If there are any engineers' reports in connection with this scheme I would ask the minister to bring them down. I would also ask him to bring down any information in possession of the department with regard to the levels, the tonnage which originates in that section, the rainfall of the area drained by this enormous river and so on.
I placed that information on the table some time ago.
We would also like to know the depth of these artesian wells.
And how much the pump cost. -

It is important to know if any engineer of standing has made a report as to the utility or the feasibility of this canal. We have heard that engineers were going to report but we have never got the concrete fact. If the minister has any written reports he should bring them down.
I have them here tonight but we are going on to consider another item.

Has the minister taken
into consideration the question of lighting these waterways. On the Scugog river from Sturgeon Lake to Lindsay there is a great deal of traffic and the river is not always properly lighted. A good part of it could be lighted by electricity but I am informed that possibly it could be lighted more cheaply by acetylene gas.
When the work on the canal is completed the question of the proper method of lighting it will have to be considered.

Would the minister bring down the report of the deputy minister upon which the Minister of Justice this evening justified the proceedings? I would also like to have a difference made between the feasibility of the mechanical construction and the utility of the work, as well as the commercial data upon which the department concluded it was wise to spend this money.

I do not know if we have all that information. I have the report made by Mr. Walsh, a prominent engineer in 1906, and I have a later report by Mr. Grant one of the best men in Canada. I have no written report from my deputy or chief engineer. The statement of the deputy was based on what the engineers have reported to him.

It would have very great
weight with this House if the substance of the information which was communicated to the Minister of Justice were communicated to us who are to criticise and to vote for this expenditure. The Minister of Justice to-night argued on what he said was the information given to him by the engineer whom*, he lauded so highly, and I am not saying anything against the laudation.
The information made to the Minister of Justice was practically the contents of these reports of engineers in whose judgment the chief engineer has confidence.

Then the Minister of
Justice as usual was wrong.
I am explaining what occurred. I have both these reports here to-night.
It was not, then, the report of the deputy minister, but the report of these engineers. The Minister of Justice represented that it was the report of the deputy minister.
The deputy minister based what he said on the reports of these two men. The report of Mr. Wash was what this House acted on, I suppose. He endorsed the scheme before Mr. Butler was chief engineer.

The hon. minister will note the unfairness of the argument of the Minister of Justice, who informed the House that he was willing to stand by the report of one of the ablest engineers in the country, that is, the deputy, Mr. Butler, and that that gentleman had reported to him that everything connected with this canal was satisfactory, virtually leaving the inference that the chief engineer had made the report on his own knowledge after having looked over the work. I think it is up. to the Minister of Justice to square himself with the House after trying to shoulder any responsibility for this canal and its non-success on an engineer of such standing as the deputy minister. If I were an engineer, I would not tolerate it for one minute unless I had made the report.
Welland canal-electrio lighting and power plant, $8,000.
What does it cost to operate this electric plant?
This work is not quite completed yet, and it is difficult to tell just what the cost is. All the locks except No. 27 are now operated by electricity.
What I want to see is how the cost compares with the cost on the Cornwall canal.
I will try to get that for my hon. friend. I think it is very much less.
Does this $8,000 finish the work?

Yes.
To widen canal near Welland, $10,000.
What is being done there?

The work that was undertaken was quite a large work. It was to enlarge and widen the canal-really to make a basin. There has been expended on it up to date about $47,000. The total estimated cost is $87,000.
Port Colborne improvements, $65,000.
We would like to have an explanation of where we are going to.

This work has been under way since 1900. A number of tenders were received, and the contract was made with Mr. GRAHAM.
Messrs. Hogan & McDonald. We are trying to make a clear navigation of 20 feet depth.
What have we now at Port Colborne?
We have 20 feet of navigation right up to the piers.
Is the elevator completed?
Yes, and we put 350,000 bushels through it last season as a test, and it worked very satisfactorily.
During the election?
No. We wanted to try it before the season of navigation closed. The vessel was the ' Midland Prince.'
What is the capacity of the elevator?	.
The storage capacity now is 800,000 bushels. It has foundations for 2,000,000 bushels.

The ' Midland Prince ' came down two or three weeks before the election. I would like to know why there was not more grain put through that elevator last fall. As I understand, it was built in order that the freight rates from Fort William and Port Arthur to Montreal might be reduced. Do the minister and his department believe that it will be operated from this out, and if so to what extent, and will it result in cheapening freight rates? I opposed the building of the elevator at Port Colborne; I have always believed that the better plan would be to deepen the Welland canal so as to permit vessels to come through to Kingston or Prescott. That would materially cheapen freight rates from Fort William to Montreal. What does the minister expect to happen in the coming year on account of the elevator being ready?

That is a large order. I do not know just what is going to happen, I hope the elevator will be busy. It has been suggested, and this is perhaps worth considering, that we ought not to be content with waiting to see what it will do but should engage some person on commission or otherwise, to induce shipments via that elevator and see if we cannot have a large volume of grain pass through it this year. The elevator is ready for business and experts say it is one of the best equipped on the continent for its size and capable of doing its work. I have been considering for some time whether it would be better just to say to the public: The elevator is there, go on and use it, or to send some person representing that elevator perhaps to the board of trade at Winnipeg to induce them to ship grain by that route and give it a

full test. I would be glad of an expression of opinion on this point.
Does not the minister think that shippers will soon realize if the elevator is any use ?
There is a difference of opinion on that. Some say the elevator will not be used unless we send some one to induce shippers to send grain through it.
Will the country be responsible for the contract ?
Oh no, if we sent a man west we might give him a certain commission for every bushel of grain he sent that way.
Why should you rival other routes ?

We built the elevator to be of some use and want to impress the public with its usefulness. I think if the public would use it one year they might be convinced of its usefulness. I agree that we could, with a larger Welland canal, rival the transportation system of any country for grain to the sea-board.
We were told it was something like Castoria, that the children cried for it.

The building of the elevator at Port Colborne seems to me to be a useful piece of work. Large boats that are unable to pass through the canal with a full cargo can unload part of their cargo at Port Colborne and so pass on to Montreal, but it would seem to me that to make the system practicable there should also be an elevator at Port Dalhousie so that the boats could take on their full cargoes there. The opinion in Port Colborne of men who are well qualified to speak is that the elevator is badly located, and that good judgment was not used in its erection. Many items under the Welland canal are very familiar to me, because during the last general election in that county our good friend the member for that county (Mr. German) issued a circular letter to his constituents in which he took credit for all the expenditures included here upon the Welland canal in addition to post offices and armouries in Welland town and Niagara Falls. I notice one item here widening the canal near Welland, $40,000. In the circular letter it was stated that one of the reasons why Mr. German should be returned was that he had succeeded in getting the government to spend $40,000 in widening the canal at this particular point for the use of a steel plant located there. The expenditures may be wise, I am not criticising them, but I think the elevator scheme is a good one if it is properly carried out, although the opinion there is that the elevator is not well located.

Although that elevator was built with the expectation that it would really complete the system between Fort William and Montreal, and that vessels would then be able to carry the grain between these two cities at a minimum cost, still I do not believe it would have that effect. I still believe that the whole solution of the question of the transportation of grain between Fort William and Montreal is to deepen the Welland canal. But we have the elevator now at Port Colborne and it will take years to deepen the Welland canal. I think every thing should be done in order that the grain from the Northwest provinces should go through via Montreal, and in addition to that any grain that we can bring from the western states via the St. Lawrence route. If the government collects charges at the elevator of any large amount it will certainly prevent grain going through that elevator and the result will be that the elevator will stand there doing nothing. I would suggest that the elevator be made practically a part of the Welland canal system and that grain should be put through that elevator at cost price. In other words, if a vessel comes there with a cargo of grain the actual cost of unloading the grain and putting it into other vessels for transportation to Montreal is all that should be charged. I could name a number of vessel owners in Canada, one of them the St. Lawrence and Chicago Forwarding Company of Toronto, which has several large vessels carrying between 200,000 and 300,000 bushels. These large vessels can go to Port Colborne and the company have several other vessels which could carry the grain from Port Colborne to Montreal. If they could put it through the Port Colborne elevator at the cost price of elevating and putting it back into their own vessels, I think it would encourage the carriage of grain from Fort William to Montreal. I would suggest that the elevator be made practically a part of the Welland canal system and that you should say to the St. Lawrence and Chicago Forwarding Company, or to the Montreal Transportation Company: If you will bring the vessels to Port Colborne and load into the smaller vessels there for transport to Montreal, we will put the grain through the elevator for just what it costs us to do the work. In this way, you will encourage bringing the grain down the St. Lawrence, instead of allowing it to go by Buffalo. These large vessels have to go to Buffalo, unless they come to Midland and send the grain by rail; if it goes by water it must go by Buffalo. I do not say finally that this would be advisable, but, I believe that it would be a good policy to pursue, to make the proposition to these transportation companies of which I have spoken.

I heartily endorse the remarks of the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. J. D. Reid). From my knowledge of this business, I have no hesitation in saying that the minister will not be disappointed so far as the elevator is concerned, for there is sufficient work of this character coming to fill all the available channels. Anybody conversant with the traffic on the great lakes knows that the additional vessel room required every year, even for mooring, for loading and unloading, amounts to virtually three-quarters of a mile. The tonnage is growing at a rate quite unknown to those who are not familiar with this business. When it comes to the last week in the fall, every port on Georgian bay and Lake Huron is congested and vessels have to be moored three and four deep and await unloading. I am heartily in accord with any expenditure that will give to this tonnage, which is growing and bound to grow like a snowball in larger percentage each year, the accommodation that it requires. I would like the minister to give me information, the next time his estimates are before us, as to the policy of the government in expenditure on these harbours and canals. Whether the expenditure is to be confined to the harbours named by the commission appointed some years ago by the government. That commission narrowed down the expenditures at the east end of the great lakes to three harbours-Parry Sound, Midland and Port Col-borne. To my mind, these gentlemen, who were not experts on transportation on the great lakes, did a great injustice to other harbours, altogether apart from the fact that if the government built piers and spent all the money they could on all the harbours, they could not keep pace with the growth of that traffic. I think that any one who takes a thoughtful interest in the welfare of the west will say that every one of these expenditures made for the accommodation of this traffic will take care of itself and will yield benefit to the country at large. Consider, for instance, the enormous terminals being built at Fort William. Up to a few years ago, you had only the Canadian Pacific Railway there. Within the last four or five years great terminals have been arranged by the Canadian Northern. In two or three years you will have the terminals of the Grand Trunk Pacific-three transcontinental lines bearing the wheat down to Port Arthur and Fort William. About $5,000,000 has been spent on harbour facilities to put the grain into the vessels. But how are you taking' care of the lower end of the spout? That is a matter the government will have to consider. The engineer of the department has given this subject a great deal of thought, and the reports of the department call attention to the question involved. I would urge the minister to con-Mr. J. D. REID.
sider the advisability of putting in the supplementary estimates items necessary for other points. The estimates this year had been cut down to Parry Sound, Midland and Port Colborne. Parry Sound has virtually ceased, in a sense, to be a great centre for a railway. It is true it has a fine harbour. But the Grand Trunk owns Parry Sound, and it owns Midland also, and I understand that their policy is to send the traffic by way of Midland. Let some of the other places have a chance to develop as terminals as well as these places. The government have done a great deal, but not more than this enormous trade demands. The traffic of the northwest and the United States is tending our way. Our port of Montreal to-day is a greater port for grain shipments than New York. That is something to be proud Qf. We must make every effort to perfect every link in this chain of communication. Let us deal with things as they exist. Let us not go into airy schemes and theories which may work out eight or ten years from now, through the building of a railway to Hudson bay or something of that kind, but let us take this up as a practical, existing business question and deal with it in that spirit. I had not intended to make these remarks, but I have every sympathy with the minister and the department, and I hope that when we next consider these estimates I shall be given the information which I have asked for.

Has the minister ever asked the Dominion Marine Association what they would suggest as to the working of this elevator? It seems to me that if he were to ask them how grain could be brought to this elevator and so to the St. Lawrence route, they would be able to make some suggestions that would be of value.
The suggestion of my hon. friend I will take up in a more thorough way, to see what these companies suggest.
Is railway connection provided with this elevator at Port Colborne?
If my hon. friend will look at the next item to be taken up, he will see that I am asking $21,000 to provide connection with the Grand Trunk sidings.
Is it intended to keep that switch so that any railway may use it? We are building it ourselves, and will let any railroad use it that wants to.
Has the minister estimated the cost of deepening the Welland canal system, and also of deepening the whole St. Lawrence system?

In the next item I am asking for a small amount to go on and

complete the surveys commenced last year, so that we could make an estimate of what the new canal will cost.
Surveys, $10,000.

We have been for some little time engaged in surveying the route, an alternative route, and trying to get what the hon. member for Renfrew (Mr. White) asks for, an estimate of what it would cost to deepen the Welland canal or build a new one.

I would ask the minister to consider that in the Welland canal he will have to cut 12 to 14 miles of living rock, and when vou come to consider the great cost of moving that rock, which runs up to about $2.50 per cubic yard at the very least, as compared with moving clay at 8 cents, he should well consider the alternative route, in view of the modern engineering science.

000.

The value of the work done there up to November 30 was $166,347. The tender was given to C. S. Boone, of Toronto, the lowest tenderer, for deepening and widening the channel at the upper end. It is under construction now. This is all above the locks.
How much do you expect it will take to carry it through?
The tender is $253,657, probably it will take more money than that.
What I would like to see done there is a little straightening of the channel between the government dock and the entrance to the canal. I think the minister has that well under consideration.
That will have to be done.

I know he has been giving a great deal of consideration to us up there, which we very much appreciate indeed, and I ask that he will generously continue the good work.
Sault Ste. MJarie canal-rebuilding north entrance pier, including dredging, $68,000.

That has to be dredged out and rebuilt. We propose to advertise for tenders and let the work to the lowest tenderer. That is the north entrance pier, which is simply rotting away. I was up there on some other business last fall, and I took a look at it. It really has to be done for the safety of navigation. I think we cannot make any mistake in not letting these things go too long where navigation is concerned.
How much dredging is there to be done?

We have not got the detailed estimate in time to give it to the House. I am asking for $68,000 to start the work. We will make a' concrete pier, a permanent work.
Quebec canals-remarking boundaries, surveys. &c., to complete, $5,560.
Didn't I see something a short time ago in the papers where some deputation from New York wanted to use these canals right through?

Really what they wanted was for us to rebuild the Chambly canal up to the Richelieu river, to give them connection between the port of Montreal and the state of New York. But that has not yet been agreed to.
Lachine canal-wall north side of Basin No., 2, $70,600.

What happened that Wall-Kerg did not get it?

I understand that the Beauharnois canal was leased to some parties for a water-power and that the government have practically nothing more to do with it.

These three votes are practically in connection with the protection of land that would otherwise be drowned. This is a dyke that has been there for years. It is to build a stone protection and to macadamize the road. This work was found to be necessary and last year we had to do some temporary work to keep the land from being flooded by water.
Are the government keeping on the lockmen and maintaining the canal?
It is leased and we do not pay any of these expenses.

How much do you get out of it?
Mr. GRAHAM, $12,000 a year.
How much do you get out of the Cataract Power company?
I will give the exact figures to-morrow. I do not like to give them from memory.
I see in the Auditor General's Report at page W-83 a payment of $7,032.31 for staff last year.
That was before the lease was executed. We do not pay anything now.
Will the minister tell me whether all of the lockmasters have been dismissed?
The lessee has taken them all over; we do not pay for them.

Since the canal was leased the lessees are paying all of the men except the overseer. This dyke which is at the head of the Beauharnois canal was built in 1852. After the canal was completed the engineers discovered that they had made a mistake in calculating the level and that instead of getting 9 feet of water they had only five or six feet. They proposed the construction of the dyke between Grand Island and the shore of the St. Lawrence at the entrance to the Beauharnois canal. This is the dyke that the minister is now asking authority to repair in order to keep the water at its proper level.
Then this dyke is being built for the benefit of those who have leased the canal?
It was bought in 1852, and it has been repaired ever since to keep the water at the proper level.

Exactly, but the canal was leased in the condition it was at that time. The government leased it to a company to be used for water-power only. Now they find that they have only five or six feet of water and they want to have this dyke repaired. They ask you to spend this money in order that you may give them nine or ten feet of water.

This has nothing more to do with lessees of the Beauharnois canal than it has to do with Timbuctoo. The same lake supplies our Soulanges canal and we must have the same level of water for it. This matter was threshed out in the House last year. There were a great many petitions received asking that the property of private individuals should be protected. If we do not repair this dyke we may spend twice as much to compensate people for land which may be drowned or flooded.
Why do not the lessees do that?
This was built fifty years ago.
They have leased the property and why should they not keep it in repair? It is they who get the benefit.

This dyke was built under a judgment of the court. We examined this question very closely an'd there is no question about the necessity of the work unless we are prepared to accept the responsibility for drowning out very many acres of land.
It is right that some one should repair it, but why should the government lease this property to a lessee and then repair it at its own expense? Why should not the lessee keep it in order?
This has nothing to do with the Beauharnois canal lease at all.
The hon. gentleman that sits behind the Minister of Justice said that it was to increase the level.
Is it part of the Beauharnois canal system?
It begins two miles above the end of the Beauharnois canal.
It is outside of the canal system?
Yes.
That is not the way we understood it.
Last year you spent $13,019.76 on the Beauharnois canal; was this expenditure prior to the execution of the lease?
Yes.

Then there will be no
more repairs?
We do not pay any repairs or any staff except the overseers who look after the locks and the repair of the lock.
This item will not ao-pear again?

No.
